items.topic: Differences between book and tax income (loss)
items.task: Identify permanent vs. temporary differences to be reported on Schedule M-3 in a given scenario.
items.stem: Kestrel Supply, Inc., a calendar-year C corporation, is preparing its 2026 Schedule M-3. Which item is a permanent book-tax difference?
options: Tax depreciation on machinery that exceeds book depreciation in the year it is placed in service
An increase in an allowance for doubtful accounts that is deductible only when accounts are written off
Prepaid rent received in December 2026 that is taxed in 2026 but recognized in book income in 2027
$25,000 of interest earned on bonds issued by a state government

why.A: Faster tax depreciation reverses in later years when book depreciation exceeds tax depreciation, so it is a temporary difference.
why.B: The reserve is deducted for tax when specific accounts are written off, so the difference reverses. It is temporary.
why.C: Income is taxed earlier than it is recorded for book purposes and the difference reverses in 2027. It is temporary.
why.D: Interest on state and local bonds is recorded in book income but never taxed, so the difference never reverses. It is a permanent difference.

items.rule_line: Interest on state and local bonds is a permanent book-tax difference because it is never taxed; accelerated depreciation and reserves are temporary.

items.topic: Differences between book and tax income (loss)
items.task: Calculate the book/tax differences to be reported on a Schedule M-1 or M-3.
items.stem: Halden Tool Co., a calendar-year C corporation, reported the following for 2026: net income per books of $412,000 after recording $86,000 of federal income tax expense; $30,000 of client meals expense, of which 50% is deductible; $4,000 of fines paid to a government agency; $9,000 of interest on state bonds; and tax depreciation that exceeds book depreciation by $22,000. What is Halden's taxable income before the net operating loss deduction and special deductions?

why.A: Leaves out the $86,000 of federal income tax expense. Federal income tax recorded in the books is not deductible and must be added back.
why.B: Start with book income of $412,000 and add back federal income tax ($86,000), the disallowed 50% of meals ($15,000) and the fines ($4,000). Subtract tax-exempt interest ($9,000) and the excess tax depreciation ($22,000): $486,000.
why.C: Adds back all $30,000 of meals. Only the nondeductible 50% ($15,000) is added back.
why.D: Adds the excess tax depreciation instead of subtracting it. Larger tax depreciation lowers taxable income relative to book income.

steps: Add federal income tax expense 86,000, nondeductible meals 30,000 x 50% = 15,000, fines 4,000
Subtract tax-exempt interest 9,000 and excess tax depreciation 22,000
items.rule_line: Schedule M-1 adds back federal income tax, disallowed meals and fines, and subtracts tax-exempt interest and excess tax depreciation.

items.topic: Differences between book and tax income (loss)
items.task: Calculate the book/tax differences to be reported on a Schedule M-1 or M-3.
items.stem: For 2026, Tallis Marine, Inc. reported net income per books of $250,000 after deducting $60,000 of federal income tax expense, a $12,000 capital loss on the sale of stock (it had no capital gains), and $5,000 of premiums on a life insurance policy covering its president, for which the corporation is the beneficiary. It had no other book-tax differences. What is Tallis's taxable income before the net operating loss deduction and special deductions?

why.A: Omits the federal income tax add-back. Federal income tax expense is not deductible in computing taxable income.
why.B: Fails to add back the capital loss. A corporation may deduct capital losses only against capital gains, so the $12,000 is not deductible this year.
why.C: Fails to add back the life insurance premiums. Premiums are nondeductible when the corporation is the direct or indirect beneficiary.
why.D: Add back federal income tax ($60,000), the capital loss that exceeds capital gains ($12,000), and the officer life insurance premiums ($5,000): $327,000.

steps: Add federal income tax 60,000, excess capital loss 12,000, officer life insurance premiums 5,000
items.rule_line: Taxable income adds back federal tax, capital losses exceeding capital gains and premiums on policies where the corporation is beneficiary.

items.task: Review a C corporation's adjusted book trial balance and supporting documentation... to determine completeness and accuracy of book/tax differences on Form 1120.
items.stem: Rowan Fabrication, Inc.'s preparer drafted its 2026 Schedule M-1 as shown. Rowan has no other differences. Which correction is needed?
exhibit: Excess of tax depreciation over book depreciation (add)
options: Remove the $8,000 of client entertainment from the add-backs, because entertainment expense is deductible at 50%
Add the $6,000 of tax-exempt interest instead of subtracting it; taxable income becomes $424,000
Remove the $70,000 of federal income tax per books, because income tax expense is deductible on the return
Subtract the $40,000 of excess tax depreciation instead of adding it; taxable income becomes $332,000

why.A: Business entertainment is not deductible at all after 2017, so the $8,000 add-back is correct. Only business meals are 50% deductible.
why.B: Tax-exempt interest is in book income but excluded from taxable income, so it is properly subtracted.
why.C: Federal income taxes are not deductible by the corporation, so the book expense must be added back. The $70,000 line is correct.
why.D: Tax depreciation above book depreciation lowers taxable income, so it is subtracted. Correct line 10: $300,000 + $70,000 + $8,000 - $6,000 - $40,000 = $332,000.

steps: Draft added the depreciation, overstating income by 2 x 40,000 = 80,000 (412,000 - 332,000)
items.rule_line: Excess tax depreciation over book depreciation is subtracted on Schedule M-1; entertainment, federal tax and tax-exempt interest are treated correctly.

items.topic: Differences between book and tax income (loss)
items.task: Identify permanent vs. temporary differences to be reported on Schedule M-3 in a given scenario.
items.stem: Which corporation must file Schedule M-3 instead of Schedule M-1 with its 2026 Form 1120?
options: Palo Foods, Inc., with total assets of $8.1 million and net income of $2 million
Denali Design, Inc., with total assets of $9.9 million and gross receipts of $30 million
Corbin Labs, Inc., with total assets of $6 million and three shareholders
Ridgeway Manufacturing, Inc., with total assets of $12.4 million at year-end

why.A: The requirement is based on total assets, not net income. Total assets under $10 million means Schedule M-1.
why.B: Gross receipts do not trigger the requirement, and $9.9 million of assets is below the $10 million threshold.
why.C: Neither the assets nor the number of shareholders reaches the threshold, so it files Schedule M-1.
why.D: A corporation with total assets of $10 million or more at the end of the year must file Schedule M-3.

items.rule_line: A corporation with total assets of $10 million or more at year-end files Schedule M-3 instead of M-1.

items.topic: Differences between book and tax income (loss)
items.task: Identify permanent vs. temporary differences to be reported on Schedule M-3 in a given scenario.
items.stem: Vireo Corp.'s 2026 book-tax differences were: $6,000 of penalties paid to a government agency, $9,000 of state bond interest, $20,000 by which tax depreciation exceeded book depreciation, $14,000 of warranty expense accrued for books but deductible only when paid, and $10,000 of business meals disallowed by the 50% limit. What total amount of these differences is temporary?

why.A: Counts only the depreciation difference. The warranty accrual also reverses when the warranty claims are paid, so it is temporary too.
why.B: This is the total of the permanent differences (penalties, state bond interest, and disallowed meals), not the temporary ones.
why.C: Only the depreciation difference ($20,000) and the warranty accrual ($14,000) reverse in later years, so $34,000 is temporary.
why.D: Adds all five differences. Three of them never reverse and are permanent.

steps: Permanent: penalties 6,000, state bond interest 9,000, meals 10,000
items.rule_line: Temporary differences reverse later, such as depreciation and warranty accruals; fines, exempt interest and disallowed meals are permanent.

items.stem: Brightwater Ltd., a C corporation, reported 2026 net income per books of $500,000 after recording $105,000 of federal income tax expense and an $18,000 provision to its allowance for doubtful accounts. Actual bad debt write-offs of specific accounts were $11,000. In December 2026 it received $30,000 of prepaid income that it must include in taxable income in 2026 but will recognize in book income in 2027. What is taxable income before the net operating loss deduction and special deductions?

why.A: Omits the $30,000 of prepaid income that is taxable in 2026 but not yet in book income.
why.B: Leaves out the $18,000 provision. Reserve additions are not deductible; only actual write-offs of specific accounts are.
why.C: Add back tax expense ($105,000) and the reserve provision ($18,000), add the prepaid income ($30,000), and subtract the actual write-offs ($11,000): $642,000.
why.D: Does not subtract the $11,000 of specific write-offs, which are deductible on the return.

steps: Add federal income tax 105,000, reserve provision 18,000, income taxed but not in books 30,000
items.rule_line: Add back federal tax and reserve additions, add taxable prepaid income and subtract actual specific write-offs.

items.topic: Differences between book and tax income (loss)
items.task: Calculate the book/tax differences to be reported on a Schedule M-1 or M-3.
items.stem: Which item is reported as an addition to net income per books on Schedule M-1?
options: Tax-exempt interest included in book income
Excess of tax depreciation over book depreciation
Life insurance proceeds on a deceased officer that are included in book income
Federal income tax expense recorded in the books

why.A: Tax-exempt interest is in book income but is not taxable, so it is subtracted.
why.B: The extra tax deduction was not charged against book income, so it is subtracted.
why.C: The proceeds are excluded from taxable income, so they are subtracted from book income.
why.D: Federal income tax expense reduces book income but is not deductible, so it is added back.

items.rule_line: Federal income tax expense in the books is added back on Schedule M-1.

items.topic: Differences between book and tax income (loss)
items.task: Calculate the book/tax differences to be reported on a Schedule M-1 or M-3.
items.stem: Marlow Textiles, Inc. paid $3,000 of annual dues to a country club for its executives and deducted them in its books. What is the tax treatment of the dues?
options: Deductible at 50% because the payment is a business meal
Deductible in full because the club is used for business purposes
Deductible only against the officers' compensation for those executives
Nondeductible in full, so the amount is added back on Schedule M-1

why.A: Dues are not a meal; the 50% limit applies to qualifying business meals, not club dues.
why.B: Business use does not make dues deductible; club dues are specifically disallowed.
why.C: There is no such rule; the dues are nondeductible to the corporation.
why.D: Club dues are not deductible at all. Because the payment reduced book income, it is added back.

items.rule_line: Country club dues are nondeductible in full and are added back on Schedule M-1.

items.stem: Tamsin Realty Corp. bought an apartment building in 2026 for use in its rental business. Over what period does MACRS recover the cost of the building?
options: 39 years using the straight-line method
40 years using the alternative depreciation system
15 years using the 150% declining balance method
27.5 years using the straight-line method

why.A: That is the recovery period for nonresidential real property such as an office building.
why.B: This applies only to property subject to the alternative depreciation system, which is not the general rule here.
why.C: Fifteen years applies to certain land improvements and qualified improvement property, not to a residential building.
why.D: Residential rental property is depreciated straight-line over 27.5 years.

items.rule_line: Residential rental property is depreciated straight-line over 27.5 years.

items.stem: For 2026, Alder Systems, Inc. had net income per books of $180,000 after recording $47,000 of federal income tax expense and $30,000 of cash charitable contributions paid in December. Under the 2026 rule, only the part of contributions that exceeds 1% of taxable income is deductible, and only the part that does not exceed 10% of taxable income, both measured on taxable income before the charitable deduction. The company has no other book-tax differences. What is Alder's taxable income before the net operating loss deduction and special deductions?

why.A: Fails to add back the $47,000 of federal income tax, understating taxable income before the charitable deduction.
why.B: Treats all $30,000 as deductible. Only the band between the 1% floor and the 10% ceiling is deductible.
why.C: Taxable income before the charitable deduction is $257,000. The ceiling is 10% x $257,000 = $25,700 and the floor is 1% x $257,000 = $2,570. Contributions ($30,000) exceed the ceiling, so the deduction is $25,700 - $2,570 = $23,130 and taxable income is $257,000 - $23,130 = $233,870.
why.D: Applies the 10% ceiling to book income instead of taxable income before the charitable deduction.

steps: Ceiling 10% x 257,000 = 25,700 is lower, so deduction = 25,700
items.law_note: OBBBA adds a 1%-of-taxable-income floor on corporate charitable deductions for tax years beginning after 2025 (10% ceiling unchanged). Testable from 2026-07-01. The stem states both limits. IRC section 170(b)(2)(A) allows only contributions in the band above 1% and up to 10% of taxable income; when contributions exceed the ceiling, the floor amount is carried forward with the excess (section 170(d)(2)(C)).
items.rule_line: Corporate charitable deductions are limited to contributions above 1% and up to 10% of taxable income before the deduction.

items.task: Calculate the book/tax differences to be reported on a Schedule M-1 or M-3.
items.stem: In 2026 Cobalt Machining, Inc. placed in service $300,000 of qualifying equipment acquired after January 19, 2025, that qualifies for 100% bonus depreciation, and it did not elect out. For books it uses straight-line over 5 years with a half-year convention (first-year book depreciation $30,000). Book net income was $600,000 after $126,000 of federal income tax expense. It has no other differences. What is taxable income before the net operating loss deduction and special deductions?

why.A: Does not add back federal income tax expense.
why.B: Subtracts the full $300,000 tax depreciation without adding back the $30,000 already deducted in book income.
why.C: Add back tax expense ($126,000) and subtract the excess of tax over book depreciation ($300,000 - $30,000 = $270,000): $456,000.
why.D: Adds the excess tax depreciation. Bonus depreciation lowers taxable income and is subtracted.

items.law_note: OBBBA (P.L. 119-21, 2025-07-04) made 100% bonus depreciation permanent for qualified property acquired after 2025-01-19. Testable from 2026-07-01. The stem states the property qualifies.
items.rule_line: Bonus depreciation lowers taxable income; subtract the excess of tax over book depreciation and add back federal tax.

items.stem: Ferrand Freight, Inc., a calendar-year corporation, is completing Schedule M-3. Its preparer classified certain 2026 differences as shown. Which classification is incorrect?
exhibit: Warranty expense accrued but not yet paid
Penalties paid to a government agency
options: Interest on state bonds is a temporary difference, not a permanent one, because the interest is later taxed on sale
The accrued warranty expense is permanent, not temporary, because the accrual is not deducted in any year
The disallowed 50% of business meals is temporary, not permanent, because it may be deducted in a later year
Penalties paid to a government agency are permanent, not temporary, because they are not deductible in any year

why.A: The draft already shows it as permanent, which is correct; the interest is never taxed.
why.B: The draft shows it as temporary, which is correct; it is deducted in a later year when paid.
why.C: The draft shows it as permanent, which is correct; the disallowed part is never deducted.
why.D: The penalties will never be deductible in any year, so nothing reverses. This is a permanent difference and the draft is wrong.

items.rule_line: Penalties paid to a government agency are permanent differences because they are never deductible.

items.topic: Differences between book and tax income (loss)
items.task: Review an entity's adjusted book trial balance and supporting documentation to identify and calculate possible book/tax differences.
items.stem: Preparing Norwood Steel, Inc.'s 2026 Form 1120, a reviewer compares the adjusted trial balance with the preparer's book-tax adjustments. The preparer already added back the fines and 50% of the meals and made no other adjustments. Which omitted adjustment is required?
exhibit: Fines paid to a government agency
Bad debt expense, specific accounts written off
Life insurance premiums, officers (corporation is beneficiary)
options: Add back the full $10,000 of business meals, not only 50%
Add back $9,000 of bad debt expense from specific accounts written off as uncollectible
Add back $5,000 of salaries paid to the officers because compensation is a permanent difference
Add back $7,000 of premiums on officer life insurance policies for which the corporation is the beneficiary

why.A: Only 50% of qualifying business meals is nondeductible, and the preparer already added it back.
why.B: Specific write-offs of business receivables are deductible when worthless, so no adjustment is needed.
why.C: Reasonable compensation is deductible, so no adjustment is required.
why.D: Premiums on a policy for which the corporation is the beneficiary are nondeductible, and the preparer did not add them back.

items.rule_line: Premiums on officer life insurance for which the corporation is beneficiary are nondeductible and must be added back.

items.topic: Differences between book and tax income (loss)
items.task: Review a C corporation's adjusted book trial balance and supporting documentation... to determine completeness and accuracy of book/tax differences on Form 1120.
items.stem: Sable Instruments, Inc.'s draft 2026 Form 1120 shows gross income of $900,000, deductions other than charitable contributions of $480,000, a charitable contribution deduction of $60,000 for cash gifts paid in 2026, and taxable income of $360,000. The corporation has no other items. Under the 2026 rule, only contributions above 1% of taxable income are deductible, and only the part that does not exceed 10% of taxable income, both measured on taxable income before the deduction. What correction should the reviewer make?
options: Limit the deduction to $37,800, making taxable income $382,200, and carry forward the $22,200 not deducted
Limit the deduction to $36,000 (10% of draft taxable income), making taxable income $384,000
Make no correction, because a corporation may deduct all charitable gifts made in cash
Limit the deduction to $37,800 and carry back the $22,200 not deducted to the two prior years

why.A: Income before the charitable deduction is $420,000. The ceiling is $42,000 and the floor is $4,200, so the deductible band is $42,000 - $4,200 = $37,800 and taxable income is $382,200. The $22,200 not deducted ($18,000 over the ceiling plus the $4,200 floor amount) carries forward up to five years, because the floor amount carries over when contributions exceed the ceiling.
why.B: Applies the 10% limit to income after the charitable deduction. The base is taxable income computed before the deduction.
why.C: Corporate charitable deductions are subject to a 1% floor and a 10% ceiling, so the full $60,000 is not deductible.
why.D: Excess corporate contributions, including the floor amount, carry forward five years; they are not carried back.

steps: Floor 1% x 420,000 = 4,200, so 55,800 is eligible; ceiling 10% x 420,000 = 42,000 is lower
items.law_note: OBBBA adds a 1%-of-taxable-income floor on corporate charitable deductions for tax years beginning after 2025 (10% ceiling unchanged). Testable from 2026-07-01. The stem states both limits. Deduction = the band above 1% and up to 10% of taxable income ($42,000 - $4,200 = $37,800); the $18,000 over the ceiling and the $4,200 floor amount ($22,200 in all) are carried forward (section 170(d)(2)(A), (C)).
items.rule_line: Corporate charitable deductions are limited to 10% of taxable income before the deduction with a 1% floor; excess carries forward five years.

items.stem: Two corporations each buy $200,000 of equipment in 2026 that qualifies for 100% bonus depreciation. Kiln Co. claims the bonus depreciation. Larch Co. elects out of bonus depreciation and uses regular MACRS, under which first-year depreciation is 20% of cost. Ignoring all other items, by how much is Kiln's 2026 taxable income lower than Larch's?

why.A: Uses Larch's first-year deduction as the difference; it is Kiln's excess deduction that matters.
why.B: Kiln deducts $200,000; Larch deducts $40,000. Kiln's taxable income is $160,000 lower in 2026, a timing difference that reverses in later years.
why.C: Compares Kiln's deduction with no deduction. Larch still deducts 20% ($40,000) in the first year.
why.D: Adds the two deductions instead of subtracting them.

items.law_note: OBBBA (P.L. 119-21, 2025-07-04) made 100% bonus depreciation permanent for qualified property acquired after 2025-01-19. Testable from 2026-07-01. The stem states the property qualifies.
items.rule_line: Bonus depreciation accelerates the deduction, so taxable income is lower by the excess over regular first-year depreciation.

items.stem: Quill Publishing, Inc. bought a $500,000 life insurance policy on its chief executive in 2023, naming the corporation as beneficiary, and paid $9,000 of premiums in 2026. The chief executive died in 2026 and the corporation received $500,000 of proceeds. Which statement correctly describes the effect on the 2026 book-tax reconciliation?
options: Both items are temporary differences that reverse when the policy is surrendered
Only the premiums are adjusted; the proceeds are taxable income and need no adjustment
Only the proceeds are adjusted; the premiums are deductible business expenses
Both items are permanent differences: add back the $9,000 premiums and subtract the $500,000 proceeds

why.A: Neither item reverses in a later year; the policy ended with the death, so both are permanent.
why.B: Life insurance proceeds paid by reason of death are generally excluded, so a subtraction is needed.
why.C: Premiums on a policy under which the corporation is beneficiary are not deductible, so they are added back.
why.D: Premiums are nondeductible and proceeds are excluded, so neither reverses. Both are permanent differences.

items.rule_line: Life insurance premiums where the corporation is beneficiary are nondeductible and death proceeds are excluded, both permanent differences.

items.topic: Differences between book and tax income (loss)
items.task: Review a C corporation's adjusted book trial balance and supporting documentation... to determine completeness and accuracy of book/tax differences on Form 1120.
items.stem: Taber Outdoor, Inc.'s books show net income of $300,000 and its filed 2026 return shows taxable income of $331,000 after adding $63,000 of federal income tax expense and subtracting $8,000 of state bond interest and $24,000 of excess tax depreciation. In reviewing, the CPA finds that book expenses include $10,000 of fines that the preparer did not add back. What is the corrected taxable income?

why.A: Subtracts the fines. Fines reduced book income but are not deductible, so they are added back.
why.B: This is the taxable income shown on the filed return; it omits the fines add-back.
why.C: The return already reconciles to $331,000; adding back the nondeductible $10,000 fines gives $341,000.
why.D: Adds the fines twice instead of once, overstating taxable income by $10,000.

items.rule_line: Fines are nondeductible and added back to taxable income, adding to the amount already reconciled.

items.topic: C corporations — computation of taxable income, tax liability and allowable credits
items.task: Calculate taxable income for a C corporation.
items.stem: Elmwood Corp., a domestic C corporation, has taxable income of $500,000 for its 2026 calendar year. What is its federal income tax before credits?

why.A: Applies a 20% deduction for qualified business income. Corporations do not receive that deduction.
why.B: Domestic C corporations pay a flat 21% on taxable income: 21% x $500,000 = $105,000.
why.C: Uses the 34% top rate that applied before 2018.
why.D: Uses the 35% rate that applied to taxable income over $10 million before 2018.

items.rule_line: Domestic C corporations pay a flat 21% federal tax on taxable income.

items.topic: C corporations — computation of taxable income, tax liability and allowable credits
items.task: Calculate taxable income for a C corporation.
items.stem: Bristol Holdings, Inc., a calendar-year C corporation, received $100,000 of dividends in 2026 from a domestic corporation in which it owns 25% of the stock. The stock was held for more than a year, and taxable income before the dividends-received deduction is well above $300,000. What is the dividends-received deduction?

why.A: Uses the 50% rate for less-than-20% ownership. At 25% ownership the 65% rate applies.
why.B: A corporation owning at least 20% but less than 80% of the payor deducts 65% of the dividend: $65,000.
why.C: Uses the 80% rate that applied to 20%-owned payors before 2018; the current rate is 65%.
why.D: The full deduction applies only to qualifying dividends within an affiliated group (80% or more ownership).

steps: Ownership 25% is at least 20% and under 80%: rate 65%
items.rule_line: The dividends-received deduction is 65% for 20% to under 80% ownership.

items.topic: C corporations — computation of taxable income, tax liability and allowable credits
items.task: Calculate taxable income for a C corporation.
items.stem: In 2026, Whitcomb Optics, Inc. received $200,000 of dividends from a domestic corporation in which it owns 10% of the stock. Whitcomb's taxable income computed before the dividends-received deduction is $150,000, and it has no net operating loss. Using the 50% dividends-received deduction rate, what is its dividends-received deduction?

why.A: This is the $50,000 of taxable income left after the full $100,000 deduction. It confuses the resulting taxable income with the deduction itself.
why.B: The deduction is the lesser of 50% of the dividends ($100,000) or 50% of taxable income before the deduction ($75,000). The $75,000 limit applies because the full deduction would not create a loss.
why.C: Applies the 65% rate to taxable income. The 65% rate applies only to 20%-owned payors, and Whitcomb owns 10%.
why.D: Ignores the taxable-income limit. The deduction cannot exceed 50% of taxable income computed before the deduction when no loss results.

steps: Full 100,000 would not create a loss (150,000 - 100,000 = 50,000), so limit applies: 75,000
items.rule_line: The DRD is the lesser of the percentage of dividends or the percentage of taxable income before the DRD, unless it creates a loss.

items.topic: C corporations — computation of taxable income, tax liability and allowable credits
items.task: Calculate taxable income for a C corporation.
items.stem: Lindqvist Capital, Inc. bought common shares of a domestic corporation 10 days before the ex-dividend date and sold them 20 days after that date. It held the shares for 30 days in total and received a $40,000 dividend. Which statement is correct about its dividends-received deduction?
options: No deduction is allowed, because the shares were not held for more than 45 days during the 91-day period around the ex-dividend date
A 50% deduction is allowed, because the shares were held for more than 30 days
A 65% deduction is allowed, because any holding period suffices for dividends from domestic corporations
The deduction is allowed but reduced in proportion to the days held

why.A: The stock must be held more than 45 days within the 91-day period beginning 45 days before the ex-dividend date. Thirty days does not qualify.
why.B: There is no 30-day rule for common stock; the required holding period is more than 45 days within the 91-day window.
why.C: The dividends-received deduction is denied unless the holding requirement is met.
why.D: The deduction is not prorated; it is either allowed in full at the applicable rate or denied.

items.rule_line: The DRD requires holding the stock more than 45 days within the 91-day period around the ex-dividend date.

items.topic: C corporations — computation of taxable income, tax liability and allowable credits
items.task: Calculate taxable income for a C corporation.
items.stem: Cascade Provisions, Inc. had these 2026 results: gross receipts from sales $2,400,000; cost of goods sold $1,300,000; salaries $500,000; depreciation $120,000; dividends of $40,000 from a domestic corporation in which it owns 10%; interest of $10,000 on state bonds; and cash contributions to charity of $25,000. Under the 2026 rule, a corporation deducts only the part of its contributions that exceeds 1% of taxable income, and the deduction cannot exceed 10% of taxable income, both measured before the charitable deduction and the dividends-received deduction. Using the 50% dividends-received deduction rate, what is Cascade's federal income tax liability?

why.A: Deducts the whole $25,000, ignoring the 1% floor, which disallows the first $5,200.
why.B: Taxable income before charity and DRD is $520,000 (state bond interest is excluded). The floor is 1% x $520,000 = $5,200, so the deduction is $25,000 - $5,200 = $19,800 (under the $52,000 ceiling). DRD is 50% x $40,000 = $20,000. Taxable income is $480,200; tax at 21% is $100,842.
why.C: Includes the $10,000 of state bond interest in taxable income. It is excluded.
why.D: Omits the dividends-received deduction of $20,000.

items.law_note: P.L. 119-21 s.70426 adds a 1% floor to the corporate charitable deduction for tax years beginning after 2025 (10% ceiling unchanged). Testable from 2026-07-01. The stem states both limits. Here the contribution ($25,000) is below the ceiling, so the $5,200 disallowed by the floor is not carried forward. (The Cornell LII copy of IRC 170 predates the amendment; confirmed against the public-law summary and practitioner guidance.)
items.rule_line: Corporate taxable income excludes state bond interest, applies the 1% charity floor and the DRD, then the 21% rate.

items.topic: C corporations — computation of taxable income, tax liability and allowable credits
items.task: Calculate taxable income for a C corporation.
items.stem: Foxglove Industries, Inc. is an accrual-basis, calendar-year corporation. Its board of directors authorized a $20,000 gift to a public charity on December 15, 2026, and the gift was paid on March 10, 2027. Foxglove makes the election available to accrual-basis corporations to treat the gift as paid when authorized. In which year may Foxglove deduct the gift, subject to the percentage limit?
options: 2027, because contributions are deductible only when paid, whatever the corporation's method
2026 only if the board approved the gift before December 1 of that year
2026 or 2027, at the corporation's choice when it files the return
2026, because the board authorized it during the year and it was paid within 3.5 months

why.A: That is the general cash-basis result. The 3.5-month election is available to accrual-basis corporations.
why.B: There is no date within the year that matters; authorization by year-end is enough.
why.C: The election has been made, so the gift is treated as paid in 2026. It is not left to be deducted in either year at the filing date.
why.D: An accrual-basis corporation may treat a gift authorized by the board during the tax year as paid in that year if actually paid by the 15th day of the fourth month after year-end.

items.law_note: IRC 170(a)(2) is an election. The stem now states that the election is made, so only 2026 is correct (before the fix, C 'either year at the corporation's choice' was also arguable).
items.rule_line: An accrual-basis corporation may treat a board-authorized gift as paid in the year authorized if paid within 3.5 months after year-end.

items.topic: C corporations — computation of taxable income, tax liability and allowable credits
items.task: Calculate taxable income for a C corporation.
items.stem: Reviewing Redwood Dynamics, Inc.'s 2026 Schedule C, a CPA sees the dividends-received deductions shown. Which item was claimed at the wrong percentage? Assume the deductions are not limited by taxable income and all holding periods are met.
options: The dividend from Delta Corp., in which Redwood owns 25%, should be deducted at 65%, not 50%
The dividend from Alpha Corp., in which Redwood owns 5%, should be deducted at 65%, not 50%
The dividend from Beta Corp., in which Redwood owns 90%, should be deducted at 65%, not 100%
The dividend from Gamma Corp., in which Redwood owns 15%, should be deducted at 100%, not 50%

why.A: Ownership of 20% or more (but under 80%) qualifies for 65%. The draft used only 50%, which understates the deduction by $6,000.
why.B: Ownership under 20% qualifies only for 50%, so the draft is right.
why.C: Beta is a member of Redwood's affiliated group (80% or more), so the 100% rate on qualifying dividends is right.
why.D: Ownership of 15% qualifies for 50%; 100% is limited to affiliated group members.

items.rule_line: The DRD is 65% for 20% to under 80% ownership, 50% below 20%, and 100% only for qualifying affiliated group dividends.

items.topic: C corporations — computation of taxable income, tax liability and allowable credits
items.task: Calculate taxable income for a C corporation.
items.stem: Sterling Bakeshop, Inc. incurred $12,000 of organizational costs to form the corporation and began business on July 1, 2026. It elected to deduct organizational costs and amortize the remainder over 180 months from the month business began. What is the total organizational cost deduction for 2026?

why.A: Amortizes the entire $12,000 and skips the $5,000 immediate deduction.
why.B: Omits amortization of the remaining $7,000 for the six months business was open.
why.C: Up to $5,000 is deducted immediately (the full $5,000 because total costs are under $50,000). The remaining $7,000 amortizes over 180 months: $7,000 / 180 x 6 months = $233. Total $5,233.
why.D: Deducts all costs. Only $5,000 may be deducted at once; the rest is amortized.

items.rule_line: Corporate organizational costs allow a $5,000 immediate deduction and amortization of the rest over 180 months from the month business begins.

items.topic: C corporations — computation of taxable income, tax liability and allowable credits
items.task: Calculate taxable income for a C corporation.
items.stem: Palisade Tools, Inc. is a calendar-year corporation that expects to owe more than $500. On what date is its first required estimated tax installment for 2026 due?
options: January 15, 2026
March 15, 2026
April 15, 2026

why.A: That is the individual final estimated payment date for the prior year, not a corporate date.
why.B: March 15 is the S corporation and partnership return due date, not a corporate installment date.
why.C: June 15 is the second corporate installment, not the first.
why.D: Corporate installments are due on the 15th day of the fourth, sixth, ninth and twelfth months of the tax year; for a calendar-year corporation the first is April 15.

items.rule_line: A calendar-year corporation's estimated tax installments are due on the 15th of the fourth, sixth, ninth and twelfth months.

items.topic: C corporations — computation of taxable income, tax liability and allowable credits
items.task: Calculate taxable income for a C corporation.
items.stem: Norland Shipping, Inc. is a calendar-year C corporation. When is its 2026 Form 1120 due, and what is the extended due date if it files a timely extension request?
options: April 15, 2027, extended to October 15, 2027
March 15, 2027, extended to September 15, 2027
April 15, 2027, extended to July 15, 2027
March 15, 2027, extended to October 15, 2027

why.A: A calendar-year corporation files by the 15th day of the fourth month after year-end, and the automatic extension is six months.
why.B: Those are the S corporation and partnership dates.
why.C: The automatic extension for corporations is six months, not three.
why.D: March 15 is the S corporation and partnership return date; the extension is right but the original due date is not.

items.rule_line: A calendar-year C corporation's Form 1120 is due April 15 with an automatic six-month extension to October 15.

items.topic: C corporations — computation of taxable income, tax liability and allowable credits
items.task: Calculate the current-year net operating or capital loss of a C corporation, and the limitations on use in the current year.
items.stem: Harbor Lantern, Inc. had a $500,000 net operating loss in 2025. In 2026 its taxable income before any net operating loss deduction is $400,000. Assuming no other loss carryovers, what is its 2026 taxable income?

why.A: Deducts 100% of taxable income. The 80% limit applies to losses arising after 2017.
why.B: A post-2017 net operating loss is deductible only up to 80% of taxable income: $320,000. Taxable income is $400,000 - $320,000 = $80,000, and $180,000 of NOL carries forward.
why.C: Subtracts income from the loss, which is not how the deduction is computed.
why.D: Uses a 50% limit; the limit is 80%.

items.rule_line: A post-2017 NOL deduction is limited to 80% of taxable income, with the rest carried forward.

items.topic: C corporations — computation of taxable income, tax liability and allowable credits
items.task: Calculate the current-year net operating or capital loss of a C corporation, and the limitations on use in the current year.
items.stem: Corvina Marketing, Inc., a C corporation, incurred a net operating loss in its 2026 tax year that is not a farming loss or an insurance company loss. Which statement describes the carryover?
options: It may be carried back two years and forward 20 years
It may be carried back five years and forward indefinitely
It may not be carried back and expires after 20 years of carryforward
It may not be carried back and may be carried forward indefinitely, subject to an 80% taxable income limit

why.A: That was the pre-2018 rule.
why.B: A five-year carryback applied only temporarily to losses arising in 2018 through 2020.
why.C: The 20-year limit applied to pre-2018 losses.
why.D: For losses arising in years beginning after 2020, there is no carryback and the carryforward has no expiration date, limited to 80% of taxable income.

items.rule_line: A post-2020 NOL has no carryback and an indefinite carryforward, limited to 80% of taxable income.

items.topic: C corporations — computation of taxable income, tax liability and allowable credits
items.task: Calculate the current-year net operating or capital loss of a C corporation, and the limitations on use in the current year.
items.stem: Quarry Ridge Corp. sold stock at a $40,000 capital loss in 2026 and had $15,000 of capital gains in the year. What is the treatment of the $25,000 net capital loss?
options: It is not deductible in 2026, and is carried back three years and forward five years as a short-term capital loss
It offsets ordinary income up to $3,000 and the remainder carries forward indefinitely
It is fully deductible against ordinary income in 2026
It is carried forward indefinitely and may not be carried back

why.A: A corporation deducts capital losses only against capital gains. The net loss is carried back three years and forward five years, treated as short-term.
why.B: The $3,000 ordinary income offset is for individuals, not corporations.
why.C: Corporate capital losses may not offset ordinary income.
why.D: A corporation's net capital loss has a three-year carryback and a five-year carryforward.

items.rule_line: A corporation deducts capital losses only against capital gains, with a three-year carryback and five-year carryforward as short-term.

items.topic: C corporations — computation of taxable income, tax liability and allowable credits
items.task: Calculate the current-year net operating or capital loss of a C corporation, and the limitations on use in the current year.
items.stem: In 2026, Dunmore Cabinets, Inc. had $300,000 of ordinary taxable income before capital transactions, a $20,000 long-term capital gain, and a $50,000 short-term capital loss. It has no prior loss carryovers. What is its 2026 federal income tax liability?

why.A: Subtracts the whole $50,000 capital loss from ordinary income and ignores the $20,000 gain.
why.B: Deducts the whole capital loss. The excess over gains is not deductible against ordinary income.
why.C: The capital loss offsets only the $20,000 capital gain. The $30,000 net loss is not deductible now. Taxable income is $300,000, and tax is 21% x $300,000 = $63,000.
why.D: Includes the capital gain without offsetting the capital loss.

steps: Capital gain 20,000 - capital loss 50,000 = net loss 30,000 (not deductible)
items.rule_line: A corporation's capital loss offsets only capital gains, not ordinary income, and taxable income is taxed at 21%.

items.topic: C corporations — computation of taxable income, tax liability and allowable credits
items.task: Calculate the current-year net operating or capital loss of a C corporation, and the limitations on use in the current year.
items.stem: Ivory Coast Imports, Inc. had a taxable loss of $200,000 in 2024, which is a net operating loss. Its taxable income before any net operating loss deduction was $150,000 in 2025 and $300,000 in 2026. It has no other carryovers. What is the taxable income for 2026?

why.A: Applies the 80% limit to 2026 income as though no NOL had been used in 2025.
why.B: Deducts the full $200,000 in 2026, ignoring the $120,000 already used in 2025.
why.C: In 2025 the deduction is limited to 80% x $150,000 = $120,000, leaving $80,000 of NOL. In 2026 the $80,000 is fully deductible (limit $240,000), so taxable income is $300,000 - $80,000 = $220,000.
why.D: Assumes the entire NOL was used in 2025 or ignores the loss carryover.

items.rule_line: The 80% NOL limit applies each year, so a partly used NOL carryover is deducted in later years against the remaining income.

items.topic: C corporations — computation of taxable income, tax liability and allowable credits
items.task: Calculate the current-year net operating or capital loss of a C corporation, and the limitations on use in the current year.
items.stem: Bayshore Analytics, Inc.'s draft 2026 Form 1120 shows taxable income before the net operating loss deduction of $400,000, a net operating loss carryforward from 2025 of $500,000, an NOL deduction of $400,000, and taxable income of $0. Bayshore has no other loss carryforwards. What correction is required?
options: Deny the deduction unless the loss is first carried back two years, so taxable income is $400,000
Limit the deduction to $200,000, so taxable income is $200,000, and carry the remaining $300,000 forward
Limit the deduction to $320,000, and let the remaining $180,000 expire after 20 years
Limit the deduction to $320,000, so taxable income is $80,000, and carry the remaining $180,000 forward

why.A: Losses from years after 2020 cannot be carried back.
why.B: Uses a 50% limit; the limit is 80%.
why.C: Post-2017 NOLs carry forward indefinitely; the 20-year limit applied to earlier losses.
why.D: The deduction is capped at 80% of taxable income ($320,000). The unused NOL carries forward without expiration.

items.rule_line: The NOL deduction is capped at 80% of taxable income and unused NOL carries forward indefinitely without carryback.

items.topic: C corporations — computation of taxable income, tax liability and allowable credits
items.task: Calculate the current-year net operating or capital loss of a C corporation, and the limitations on use in the current year.
items.stem: Maple Crest Corp. has a $60,000 net capital loss in 2026 and no capital gains. In 2023, 2024 and 2025 it had net capital gains of $20,000, $25,000 and $40,000. In 2027 it expects a $30,000 capital gain. Which statement about the loss is correct?
options: The loss is carried back to 2023 first, then to 2024 and 2025, as a short-term loss; any remainder carries forward five years
The loss is deductible in 2026 against ordinary income up to $3,000, and the rest carries forward indefinitely
The loss is carried forward only, so it offsets the $30,000 gain in 2027 and the rest expires later
The loss is carried back to 2025 first, then to 2024 and 2023, to the extent of gains in those years

why.A: A corporate net capital loss is carried back to the third preceding year first, then the second and first, and any excess is carried forward five years.
why.B: The $3,000 offset is available to individuals only.
why.C: A corporation must first carry the loss back three years; it may carry forward only what remains.
why.D: The carryback goes to the earliest year first (the third preceding year), then progresses toward the loss year.

items.rule_line: A corporate net capital loss carries back to the third preceding year first, then the second and first, with the rest carried forward five years.

items.topic: C corporations — computation of taxable income, tax liability and allowable credits
items.task: Calculate the credits allowable as a reduction to tax for a C corporation.
items.stem: In 2026, Juniper Hardware, Inc. has net income tax before credits of $200,000, general business credits of $250,000, and no alternative minimum tax or other minimum tax liability (tentative minimum tax is zero). The limitation is net income tax minus 25% of net regular tax over $25,000. What general business credit may Juniper claim in 2026?

why.A: Takes 25% of the entire tax instead of the tax over $25,000.
why.B: The credit cannot exceed net income tax minus 25% of the tax over $25,000: $200,000 - 25% x $175,000 = $156,250. The other $93,750 is carried over.
why.C: Allows the credits to reduce tax to zero. The 25% rule requires some tax to remain.
why.D: Claims all credits without applying the limitation.

items.rule_line: The general business credit cannot exceed net income tax minus 25% of net regular tax over $25,000.

items.topic: C corporations — computation of taxable income, tax liability and allowable credits
items.task: Calculate the credits allowable as a reduction to tax for a C corporation.
items.stem: Otter Point Corp. cannot use all of its general business credit in 2026 because of the annual limitation. How are unused general business credits treated?
options: Carried back two years and carried forward 20 years
Carried forward only, for up to five years
Refunded in cash to the corporation in the following year
Carried back one year and carried forward up to 20 years

why.A: There is no two-year carryback for the general business credit.
why.B: The carryforward is 20 years, and a one-year carryback applies first.
why.C: General business credits are not refundable.
why.D: Unused general business credits are carried back one year and then forward up to 20 years.

items.rule_line: Unused general business credits carry back one year and forward up to 20 years, and are not refundable.

items.topic: C corporations — computation of taxable income, tax liability and allowable credits
items.task: Calculate the credits allowable as a reduction to tax for a C corporation.
items.stem: Crestline Motors, Inc. had 2026 worldwide taxable income of $1,000,000, of which $300,000 was from foreign sources, all in a single category. It paid $80,000 of foreign income taxes. U.S. tax before credits is 21% of taxable income. What foreign tax credit may it claim?

why.A: The credit is limited to U.S. tax multiplied by foreign-source income divided by worldwide income: $210,000 x 30% = $63,000, which is less than the $80,000 paid.
why.B: Claims all foreign taxes paid, ignoring the limitation.
why.C: Uses the domestic-income ratio (70%) instead of the foreign-source ratio.
why.D: Uses the entire U.S. tax, ignoring the ratio of foreign to worldwide income.

items.rule_line: The foreign tax credit is limited to U.S. tax times foreign-source income over worldwide income.

items.topic: C corporations — computation of taxable income, tax liability and allowable credits
items.task: Calculate the credits allowable as a reduction to tax for a C corporation.
items.stem: Which credit is one of the components of the current-year general business credit?
options: The research credit
The foreign tax credit
The credit for prior-year alternative minimum tax paid by an individual
The credit for federal income tax withheld on wages

why.A: The research credit is among the credits combined in the general business credit.
why.B: The foreign tax credit is a separate credit with its own limitation and is not part of the general business credit.
why.C: That credit belongs to individuals and is unrelated to business credits.
why.D: Withholding is a payment credit and is not a business credit.

items.rule_line: The research credit is part of the general business credit; the foreign tax credit and withholding are separate.

items.topic: C corporations — computation of taxable income, tax liability and allowable credits
items.task: Calculate the credits allowable as a reduction to tax for a C corporation.
items.stem: Draft 2026 Form 1120 workpapers for Linden Rail Supply, Inc. claim the full available general business credit. Linden has no minimum tax liability, and the one-year carryback should be ignored. Which correction is required?
exhibit: Net income tax before general business credit
options: Limit the credit to $150,000, so tax due is $50,000, and carry the unused $100,000 forward
Limit the credit to $200,000, so tax due is $0, and carry the unused $50,000 forward
Limit the credit to $156,250 and refund the unused $93,750 in cash
Limit the credit to $156,250, so tax due is $43,750, and carry the unused $93,750 forward

why.A: Takes 25% of the entire tax rather than only the tax over $25,000.
why.B: This treats the credit as able to eliminate the tax. The 25% rule leaves tax payable for a corporation with tax over $25,000.
why.C: General business credits are not refundable; unused amounts are carried to other years.
why.D: The limit is $200,000 - 25% x ($200,000 - $25,000) = $156,250. Some tax must remain, and unused credits carry forward.

items.rule_line: The general business credit limit leaves some tax payable, and unused credits carry to other years rather than being refunded.

items.topic: C corporations — state and local tax issues
items.task: Define the general concept and rationale of nexus with respect to state and local taxation.
items.stem: Sparrow Outdoor Gear, Inc. sells camping equipment (tangible goods) into State Q. Which of Sparrow's activities in State Q goes beyond the protection of the federal statute limiting state income taxation of interstate sales and can create income tax nexus?
options: Employees repair defective products at customers' sites in State Q
Sales representatives solicit orders that are approved and shipped from outside State Q
Sales representatives distribute free product samples and catalogs to prospective customers
Sparrow mails promotional email offers to residents of State Q

why.A: Repair and maintenance services exceed mere solicitation of orders, so the protection does not apply and nexus can exist.
why.B: Solicitation of orders for tangible goods, with approval and shipment from outside the state, is the activity protected from state income tax.
why.C: Delivering samples and catalogs is part of solicitation and remains protected.
why.D: Advertising by mail or email is solicitation and remains protected.

cite.ref: Dept. of Revenue v. William Wrigley, Jr., Co.

items.rule_line: Repairing products at customers' sites exceeds protected solicitation of orders and can create state income tax nexus.

items.topic: C corporations — state and local tax issues
items.task: Define the general concept and rationale of nexus with respect to state and local taxation.
items.stem: Mira Learning Co., an online course seller with no offices, employees or property in State R, made $350,000 of sales to State R customers in 2026. State R requires remote sellers with more than $100,000 of sales into the state to collect sales tax. Which statement is correct?
options: Mira has no nexus, because sales tax collection requires a physical presence in the state
Mira has nexus only if it also has employees or property in State R
Mira has nexus only after it has made sales in State R for three consecutive years
Mira has economic nexus and must collect State R sales tax, even without a physical presence

why.A: That was the rule before the Wayfair decision; physical presence is no longer required.
why.B: A physical presence is not required when an economic threshold is exceeded.
why.C: There is no three-year requirement; the state's threshold applies to the current or prior year.
why.D: Under the Wayfair decision, a state may impose collection duties on remote sellers that exceed a reasonable economic threshold.

items.rule_line: Economic nexus under Wayfair lets a state require collection from remote sellers above a sales threshold without physical presence.

items.topic: C corporations — state and local tax issues
items.task: Define the general concept and rationale of apportionment and allocation with respect to state and local taxation.
items.stem: Greenfield Tooling, Inc. operates in several states. It also earns interest on a reserve fund that is unrelated to its operations. Which statement describes the standard state treatment of these two income types?
options: Both are allocated entirely to the state in which the corporation is incorporated
Both are apportioned among the states using the same three-factor formula
Business income is apportioned by formula; nonbusiness income such as this interest is allocated to a specific state
Business income is allocated to a specific state; nonbusiness income is apportioned by formula

why.A: Business income of a multistate company is divided by formula, not assigned to one state.
why.B: Nonbusiness income is generally allocated, not apportioned.
why.C: Apportionment divides business income using factors, while allocation assigns nonbusiness income (interest, rents, gains) to a single state, often the commercial domicile.
why.D: The reverse of the standard treatment.

items.rule_line: Multistate business income is apportioned by formula, while nonbusiness income is allocated to a specific state.

items.topic: C corporations — state and local tax issues
items.task: Calculate state taxable income using the applicable apportionment factors given a specific scenario.
items.stem: Tern Logistics, Inc. has $800,000 of business income. State S apportions business income using only a sales factor. Tern's total sales are $10,000,000 including $2,000,000 sold to State S customers. Its property factor for State S is 25% and its payroll factor is 40%. What business income is apportioned to State S?

why.A: A single sales factor uses only sales: $2,000,000 / $10,000,000 = 20%. State S apportioned income is 20% x $800,000 = $160,000.
why.B: Uses only the property factor.
why.C: Averages the three factors equally, though State S uses only sales.
why.D: Uses only the payroll factor.

items.rule_line: Under a single sales factor, apportioned income equals the state's sales share times business income.

items.topic: C corporations — state and local tax issues
items.task: Calculate state taxable income using the applicable apportionment factors given a specific scenario.
items.stem: Ashby Forge, Inc. has $800,000 of business income. State T uses a three-factor formula that weights sales twice as much as property or payroll (sales weighted double). Ashby's State T factors are: sales 20%, property 25% and payroll 40%. What business income is apportioned to State T?

why.A: Uses only the sales factor.
why.B: Divides by four without doubling the sales factor.
why.C: The weighted average is (2 x 20% + 25% + 40%) / 4 = 26.25%. Apportioned income is 26.25% x $800,000 = $210,000.
why.D: Averages the factors equally, ignoring the double weight on sales.

items.rule_line: A double-weighted sales formula averages 2 x sales plus property and payroll over four, then multiplies by business income.

items.topic: C corporations — state and local tax issues
items.task: Calculate state taxable income using the applicable apportionment factors given a specific scenario.
items.stem: Delmar Textiles, Inc. reported the following for State U: business income of $600,000, of which 25% is apportioned to State U under the state's formula, and $40,000 of rental income from a nonbusiness building located in State U, which is allocated entirely to State U. What is Delmar's State U taxable income before any state adjustments?

why.A: Omits the allocated nonbusiness rental income.
why.B: Apportions the nonbusiness rent by formula. Nonbusiness income is allocated to a specific state, not apportioned.
why.C: Business income apportioned is 25% x $600,000 = $150,000. Add the allocated nonbusiness rent ($40,000): $190,000.
why.D: Assigns all income to State U with no apportionment of business income.

items.rule_line: State taxable income equals formula-apportioned business income plus nonbusiness income allocated to that state.

items.topic: C corporations — state and local tax issues
items.task: Calculate state taxable income using the applicable apportionment factors given a specific scenario.
items.stem: Kessler Optics, Inc. has $500,000 of taxable income and operates in both State A and State B. Its factors in each state are: sales 10%, property 40% and payroll 40%. State A imposes a 5% tax using a single sales factor. State B imposes a 4% tax using an equally weighted three-factor formula. Which statement compares the two taxes correctly?
options: State B's tax exceeds State A's by $3,500
State A's tax exceeds State B's by $3,500 because its rate is higher
The two taxes are equal because both states use the same taxable income
State B's tax exceeds State A's by $1,000

why.B: A higher rate does not offset State A's much smaller factor: State A's tax is $2,500 and State B's is $6,000.
why.C: The apportionment formulas and rates differ, so the taxes differ.
why.D: Uses a 10% factor for both states; State B's equally weighted factor is 30%.

items.rule_line: State tax depends on each state's apportionment formula and rate applied to the same taxable income.

items.topic: C corporations — state and local tax issues
items.task: Define the general concept and rationale of nexus with respect to state and local taxation.
items.stem: For federal income tax purposes, how does a C corporation treat the state income taxes it pays in 2026?
options: It may not deduct them, because state taxes are not business expenses
It deducts them only up to the individual cap on state and local taxes
It claims a credit against federal tax equal to the state taxes paid
It deducts them as ordinary business expenses, and the individual state and local tax cap does not apply

why.A: State income taxes are deductible taxes paid in carrying on a trade or business.
why.B: The cap applies only to individuals' itemized deductions.
why.C: State taxes are deducted, not credited.
why.D: State and local income taxes are deductible by a corporation as a business expense. The cap on state and local tax deductions applies only to individuals.

items.rule_line: A C corporation deducts state income taxes as a business expense, and the individual SALT cap does not apply.

items.stem: Adam Lindner transferred land (adjusted basis $40,000, fair market value $100,000) to a new corporation in exchange for stock worth $90,000 and $10,000 in cash. Adam controls the corporation immediately after the exchange. What gain does Adam recognize?

why.A: Assumes full nonrecognition; receipt of cash (boot) triggers gain up to the boot.
why.B: Gain is recognized to the extent of boot received: the lesser of the realized gain ($60,000) and the cash ($10,000) is $10,000.
why.C: Compares only the stock received with basis, ignoring the cash and the limit on recognized gain.
why.D: Recognizes the entire realized gain, though a transfer to a controlled corporation defers gain not matched by boot.

items.rule_line: On a transfer to a controlled corporation, gain is recognized only to the extent of boot received, up to realized gain.

The corporation's basis is $60,000, the gain that was not recognized

why.A: Nets current earnings against the deficit. Current earnings and profits are tested separately for the year.
why.B: Uses the amount in excess of current earnings and profits, which is the return of capital, not the dividend.
why.C: A distribution is a dividend to the extent of current earnings and profits, even when accumulated earnings and profits are negative: $50,000.

why.B: The first $20,000 is a dividend, the next $50,000 reduces basis to zero, and the remaining $20,000 is capital gain.
why.C: Ignores the $20,000 dividend and treats everything over basis as gain.

items.stem: For 2026, Wren Valley, Inc. distributed $90,000 in cash to its only shareholder, Owen Pruitt. The corporation's current and accumulated earnings and profits total $20,000, and Owen's stock basis is $50,000. Owen's draft return reports the entire $90,000 as a qualified dividend. Which correction is needed?
options: Report a $20,000 dividend and $70,000 of return of capital, with no gain
Report $40,000 of dividend and $50,000 of return of capital
Report a $20,000 dividend, apply $50,000 to reduce basis to $0, and report $20,000 of capital gain
Report no dividend, because the distribution is a return of capital to the extent of basis

why.A: Return of capital cannot exceed basis; the amount over basis is gain.
why.B: Overstates the dividend; only the $20,000 of earnings and profits is a dividend.
why.C: The distribution is a dividend to the extent of earnings and profits, then a nontaxable reduction of basis, then gain.
why.D: Earnings and profits are exhausted first as dividends before basis is reduced.

items.rule_line: A distribution is a dividend to the extent of E&P, then a return of basis, then capital gain.

A deductible travel expense for the corporation and no income to Jill
A loan from the corporation that is taxed only if repaid
Compensation to Jill that is deductible by the corporation and taxable to Jill

why.B: Personal expenses of a shareholder are not deductible business expenses.
why.C: Without an obligation to repay, the payment is a distribution.

why.B: Uses the shareholder's basis as the gain.
why.C: In a complete liquidation the shareholder is treated as selling the stock: amount received $250,000 minus basis $80,000 = $170,000 long-term capital gain.

The corporation recognizes a $300,000 gain, and the shareholders take a $100,000 basis

The corporation recognizes a $300,000 gain, and the shareholders take a $400,000 basis

why.A: That is the result for a qualifying subsidiary liquidation into a corporate parent, not for individual shareholders.

Tilden recognizes gain on all of the land, and both Parent and Ray recognize gain or loss on their stock
Parent recognizes no gain; Tilden recognizes gain on the land distributed to Ray, who recognizes gain or loss on his stock
Parent recognizes gain on its share of the land, and Ray recognizes nothing until he sells the land he received

why.A: The nonrecognition rule covers only the corporate parent's share; Ray's distribution is taxable.
why.B: Distributions to the 80%-or-more corporate owner are tax-free at both levels.
why.C: The 80% parent qualifies for tax-free treatment on its share, while the distribution to the minority holder is taxable at both the corporate and shareholder level.
why.D: Parent qualifies for nonrecognition, and Ray is taxed on liquidation.

items.rule_line: A subsidiary liquidation is tax-free only for the 80% corporate parent's share; the minority holder's share is taxable at both levels.

The parent must own more than 50% of the voting power of the subsidiary
The parent must own at least 80% of the subsidiary's voting power, regardless of value
The parent must own at least 20% of the subsidiary and control the board

why.A: An affiliated group requires a common parent owning at least 80% of both vote and value of each includible subsidiary.
why.B: A majority vote is not enough; 80% of vote and value is required.
why.C: Both voting power and value must reach 80%.

The parent includes the full $100,000 as income, because dividends from a subsidiary are taxable to it
The parent excludes the dividend and increases its stock basis in the subsidiary by that amount
The dividend is excluded from consolidated taxable income, and the parent reduces its basis in the subsidiary

items.stem: Briar Creek, Inc. wants to elect S status. It has 95 unrelated individual shareholders, plus 20 more shareholders who are all lineal descendants of one common ancestor (or their spouses or former spouses). All are U.S. residents. Does Briar Creek meet the shareholder-count limit?
options: Yes, because the family members are treated as one shareholder, so it has 96 shareholders
No, because it has 115 shareholders, which exceeds the limit of 100
No, because family members may be aggregated only if they file a written election
Yes, because the limit applies only to shareholders with voting stock

why.A: All members of a family (common ancestor and lineal descendants and their spouses) are treated as one shareholder for the 100-shareholder limit.
why.B: The family aggregation rule reduces the count to 96.
why.C: Family members are aggregated automatically; no election is needed.
why.D: The limit counts shareholders, not voting shareholders.

items.stem: Ferro Components, Inc., an S corporation, has two arrangements under consideration. Which one would create a second class of stock and terminate the S election?

A one-year disproportionate distribution that the governing documents do not authorize
A shareholder loan that meets the straight-debt safe harbor
Class B shares that entitle the holder to twice the per-share liquidation proceeds of Class A shares

why.A: Voting differences alone are allowed.
why.B: Disproportionate distributions do not create a second class if the governing provisions give identical rights.
why.C: Straight debt meeting the safe harbor is not treated as a second class of stock.
why.D: Shares with different rights to distribution or liquidation proceeds create a second class of stock.

items.rule_line: Shares with different distribution or liquidation rights create a second class of stock, while voting differences alone do not.

A domestic corporation with accumulated earnings and profits from earlier C years

why.B: Only banks that use the reserve method are ineligible.
why.C: Insurance companies taxed under subchapter L are ineligible corporations.

items.stem: Lakeshore Ceramics, Inc. was formed on February 1, 2026. It issued stock, acquired assets and began business on that day. It wants S status to apply from its first day. By what date must Form 2553 be filed, with all shareholders consenting?
options: April 15, 2026, the 15th day of the third month
March 15, 2026, the 15th day of the third month of a calendar year
December 31, 2026, the last day of the tax year
May 15, 2026, the 15th day of the fourth month of the tax year

why.A: The election must be made no later than the 15th day of the third month of the tax year to be effective for that year.
why.B: March 15 applies to a corporation with a January 1 start; here the tax year began February 1.
why.C: Filing after the 15th day of the third month makes the election effective for the following year.
why.D: That is the 15th day of the fourth month, which is one month too late.

items.rule_line: Form 2553 must be filed by the 15th day of the third month of the tax year to be effective for that year.

items.topic: S corporations — eligibility and election

items.stem: Ridgecrest Homes, Inc., an S corporation, has 1,000 shares outstanding: 500 voting and 500 nonvoting. Carla holds 300 voting and 100 nonvoting shares. Dev holds 100 voting and 300 nonvoting shares. Others hold the remaining 200 shares. Who can revoke the S election without the consent of anyone else?
options: Carla alone, because she holds 60% of the voting shares
Dev alone, because he holds 60% of the nonvoting shares
Any single shareholder may revoke, since the election requires unanimous consent to make but not to revoke
Carla and Dev together, who hold 80% of all shares

why.A: Revocation is measured on all shares, including nonvoting ones. Carla holds only 40% of all shares.
why.B: Dev also holds only 40% of all shares.
why.C: Revocation requires the consent of holders of more than half the shares.
why.D: A revocation requires consent of shareholders holding more than half of all shares, voting and nonvoting. Together they hold 80% of all shares.

items.rule_line: Revoking an S election requires consent of holders of more than half of all shares, voting and nonvoting.

items.stem: Cedar Hollow, Inc. is an S corporation that was a C corporation earlier and still has accumulated earnings and profits. Passive investment income exceeded 25% of gross receipts in each of 2024, 2025 and 2026. When does its S status terminate?
options: On December 31, 2024, after the first year of excess passive income
On the date passive income first exceeded 25%, in 2026
On January 1, 2027, the first day of the tax year after the third consecutive year
It does not terminate; the corporation pays only a corporate-level tax each year

why.A: Three consecutive years are required.
why.B: Termination is effective on the first day of the next tax year, not the date the threshold is crossed.
why.C: The election terminates on the first day of the first tax year beginning after the third consecutive tax year in which the corporation had accumulated earnings and profits and excess passive income.
why.D: The corporate-level tax applies each year, but three consecutive years also terminate the election.

items.rule_line: An S election terminates on the first day of the year after three consecutive years of excess passive income with accumulated E&P.

items.stem: On September 10, 2026, Sofia Reyes, a shareholder of a calendar-year S corporation, sold 20% of the stock to a partnership. Before then the corporation met all requirements. From what date is the corporation a C corporation?
options: September 10, 2026, the date of the terminating event
January 1, 2026, the start of the year
January 1, 2027, the start of the next year
December 31, 2026, the end of the year

why.A: Ceasing to be a small business corporation terminates the election on the day the event occurs. The year splits into S and C short years.
why.B: Termination is not retroactive; it is effective on the day of the event.
why.C: Termination for ineligibility is effective on the date of the event, not the next year.
why.D: The termination date is the event date, not year-end.

items.rule_line: An S election terminates on the day the corporation ceases to qualify, splitting the year into S and C short years.

items.stem: An S corporation election terminated effective in 2026, so 2026 is the corporation's first C corporation year. Absent consent from the IRS, what is the earliest year for which it may elect S status again?

2029, the third year after termination
2036, ten years after termination
2031, the fifth taxable year after the first C corporation year

why.B: The waiting period is five taxable years, not three.
why.C: There is no ten-year rule; the wait is five taxable years.
why.D: A corporation may not re-elect S status before its fifth taxable year after the first year the termination took effect, without IRS consent.

items.rule_line: A corporation whose S election terminated may not re-elect before its fifth taxable year after the first C year without IRS consent.

why.C: An entity taxed as a partnership cannot be an S corporation shareholder, so the election is invalid.
why.D: A resident alien is a permitted shareholder; only nonresident aliens are excluded.

items.rule_line: Entities taxed as partnerships cannot be S corporation shareholders, while citizens, grantor trusts and resident aliens can.

items.topic: S corporations — determination of ordinary business income (loss) and separately stated items
items.task: Calculate ordinary business income (loss) and separately stated items for an S corporation for tax purposes.
items.stem: Tamarack Design, Inc., an S corporation, had 2026 revenue of $900,000, cost of goods sold of $400,000, wages of $200,000 and regular depreciation of $50,000. It also had a $30,000 immediate expensing deduction, a $10,000 charitable contribution, $6,000 of interest income, $4,000 of tax-exempt interest and a $20,000 long-term capital gain. What is its ordinary business income?

why.A: Deducts the immediate expensing amount in ordinary income; it is separately stated.
why.B: Deducts the charitable contribution in ordinary income; it is a separately stated item.
why.C: Revenue less COGS, wages and depreciation is $250,000. The immediate expensing deduction, charitable gift, interest, tax-exempt interest and capital gain are separately stated.
why.D: Includes interest income and the capital gain, which are separately stated to shareholders.

steps: Separately stated: expensing 30,000, charity 10,000, interest 6,000, tax-exempt interest 4,000, capital gain 20,000
items.rule_line: S corporation ordinary income excludes separately stated items such as section 179, charity, interest and capital gains.

items.topic: S corporations — determination of ordinary business income (loss) and separately stated items
items.task: Calculate ordinary business income (loss) and separately stated items for an S corporation for tax purposes.
items.stem: Falcon Ridge, Inc., a calendar-year S corporation that has not elected to close its books, had $365,000 of ordinary business income for 2026. Wes Palmer owned 40% of the stock from January 1 through March 31 and sold all of it on March 31. How much ordinary business income is allocated to Wes?

why.A: Income is allocated per share per day. Wes owned 40% for 90 days (January 1 through March 31, the day of sale counting as a day of ownership): $365,000 x 90/365 x 40% = $36,000.
why.B: Uses a half-year holding period instead of 90 days.
why.C: Prorates by days but does not apply Wes's 40% ownership.
why.D: Allocates 40% of the full year, ignoring that Wes owned the stock for only 90 days.

items.law_note: A seller is treated as the shareholder for the day of disposition (Reg. 1.1377-1(a)(2)(ii)). The stem originally said the sale was on April 1 (91 days, $36,400); it now says March 31 so the count is exactly 90 days.
items.rule_line: S corporation income is allocated per share per day of ownership, including the sale date.

items.topic: S corporations — determination of ordinary business income (loss) and separately stated items
items.task: Calculate ordinary business income (loss) and separately stated items for an S corporation for tax purposes.
items.stem: Which deduction may an S corporation claim in computing its ordinary business income?
options: Wages paid to employees
The dividends-received deduction
A net operating loss deduction
The federal income tax on its ordinary income

why.A: An S corporation deducts ordinary and necessary business expenses such as wages.
why.B: S corporations cannot claim the corporate dividends-received deduction; dividends pass through.
why.C: S corporation losses pass through to shareholders; the entity has no net operating loss deduction.
why.D: An S corporation generally pays no federal income tax on its ordinary income, so there is nothing to deduct.

items.rule_line: An S corporation deducts ordinary business expenses like wages, but not the DRD, an NOL or federal income tax.

items.topic: S corporations — determination of ordinary business income (loss) and separately stated items
items.task: Calculate ordinary business income (loss) and separately stated items for an S corporation for tax purposes.
items.stem: Which of these items must an S corporation state separately on Schedule K-1 rather than include in ordinary business income?
options: Wages paid to employees
Cost of goods sold
Regular depreciation on business equipment
Charitable contributions made by the corporation

why.A: Wages are ordinary business deductions included in box 1.
why.B: Cost of goods sold is part of ordinary business income.
why.C: Ordinary depreciation is a business deduction included in box 1; only the expensing election is separately stated.
why.D: Charitable contributions are separately stated because shareholders' deductions depend on individual limits.

items.rule_line: An S corporation separately states items like charitable contributions that depend on each shareholder's own limits; wages, COGS and regular depreciation stay in box 1.

items.topic: S corporations — determination of ordinary business income (loss) and separately stated items
items.task: Calculate ordinary business income (loss) and separately stated items for an S corporation for tax purposes.
items.stem: Northfield Print, Inc., an S corporation, paid $12,000 of health insurance premiums in 2026 for Grace Tull, who owns 30% of the stock and works full time for the company. How is the payment treated?
options: The corporation deducts it and Grace excludes it from income as an ordinary employee fringe benefit of the company
The corporation cannot deduct it, because it is a distribution to a shareholder rather than compensation
The corporation deducts it and includes it in Grace's wages; Grace may take the self-employed health insurance deduction
The payment is included in Grace's wages and is subject to FICA tax like other wages

why.A: Fringe benefit exclusions do not apply to more-than-2% shareholders.
why.B: Premiums are deductible compensation-type expenses if included in wages.
why.C: Premiums for a more-than-2% shareholder-employee are wages for income tax purposes (not FICA), deductible by the corporation, and deductible by the shareholder on Schedule 1.
why.D: Premiums paid under a plan for a more-than-2% shareholder-employee are reported in box 1 wages but are not FICA wages, so the statement that they are subject to FICA like other wages is wrong.

items.rule_line: Health premiums for a more-than-2% S shareholder-employee are included in wages but not FICA, and deductible by the corporation and shareholder.
