items.task: Review federal Form 1120S and supporting documentation to determine completeness and accuracy of classification of items.
items.stem: A preparer classified the following 2026 items of Delta Ridge, Inc., an S corporation, on Form 1120-S and Schedule K. Which classification is incorrect?
options: The $5,000 cash charitable contribution should be separately stated, not deducted in box 1
The $15,000 long-term capital gain should not be separately stated
The $3,000 of interest income on savings should be included in box 1
The $40,000 of regular depreciation should be separately stated

why.A: Charitable contributions are separately stated items and should not reduce ordinary business income.
why.B: Capital gains are separately stated on Schedule K; the draft is right.
why.C: Portfolio interest is separately stated; the draft is right.
why.D: Regular MACRS depreciation is an ordinary business deduction, so the draft is right.

items.rule_line: Charitable contributions are separately stated, while regular depreciation stays in ordinary income and capital gains and interest are separately stated.

items.task: Review and resolve discrepancies identified by automated diagnostic and validation checks for Form 1120S.
items.stem: An automated check on Sedge Bay, Inc.'s 2026 Form 1120-S flags that shareholder box 1 amounts do not equal Schedule K line 1, which shows $200,000. Shareholders and ownership all year: Amy 50%, Ben 30%, Cal 20%. The Schedule K-1s show box 1 of $100,000 for Amy, $60,000 for Ben and $30,000 for Cal. Which correction resolves the discrepancy?
options: Change Amy's box 1 amount to $110,000
Change Ben's box 1 amount to $70,000
Reduce Schedule K line 1 to $190,000
Change Cal's box 1 amount to $40,000

why.A: Amy's 50% share is $100,000, which is correct.
why.B: Ben's 30% share is $60,000, which is correct.
why.C: The Schedule K total is the source amount; the error is in the shareholder allocation.
why.D: Cal owned 20% all year, and 20% of $200,000 is $40,000. Amy and Ben are correct.

items.rule_line: S corporation ordinary income is allocated to shareholders by ownership percentage, so each K-1 must sum to Schedule K.

items.topic: S corporations — determination of ordinary business income (loss) and separately stated items
items.task: Calculate the impact of current year operations on an S corporation's accumulated adjustments account.
items.stem: For 2026, Oakhaven Supply, Inc., an S corporation, began the year with an accumulated adjustments account (AAA) of $40,000. It had ordinary business income of $120,000, a long-term capital gain of $10,000, tax-exempt interest of $5,000, nondeductible expenses of $3,000, charitable contributions of $4,000 and cash distributions of $50,000. What is AAA at year-end?

why.A: AAA increases by ordinary income and capital gain and decreases by nondeductible expenses, charitable gifts and distributions: $113,000. Tax-exempt income affects a separate account.
why.B: Adds tax-exempt interest to AAA. That income adjusts the other adjustments account instead.
why.C: Omits the reductions for nondeductible expenses and charitable contributions.
why.D: Omits the reduction for the $50,000 of distributions.

steps: Add ordinary income 120,000 and capital gain 10,000
Subtract nondeductible expenses 3,000, charitable contributions 4,000, distributions 50,000
items.rule_line: AAA increases with ordinary income and capital gains and decreases with nondeductible expenses, charity and distributions; tax-exempt income is excluded.

items.topic: S corporations — determination of ordinary business income (loss) and separately stated items
items.task: Calculate the impact of current year operations on an S corporation's accumulated adjustments account.
items.stem: Riverbend Grocers, Inc., an S corporation, had an AAA of $20,000 at the beginning of 2026, and an ordinary business loss of $30,000 for the year. During the year it made a $25,000 cash distribution. The corporation has no accumulated earnings and profits. How much of the distribution is treated as coming from AAA?

why.A: Reduces AAA by the loss first. Distributions ignore the net negative adjustment for the year.
why.B: Uses the excess of the distribution over AAA, not the AAA amount.
why.C: For distribution purposes AAA is figured without the net negative adjustment for the year, so the full beginning AAA of $20,000 is available. The remaining $5,000 is applied against stock basis.
why.D: Treats the entire distribution as from AAA, which is only $20,000.

steps: AAA available for distributions (ignoring net negative adjustment) = 20,000
Amount treated as from AAA = min(25,000, 20,000) = 20,000
items.rule_line: For distributions, AAA is computed without regard to the net negative adjustment for the year.

items.topic: S corporations — determination of ordinary business income (loss) and separately stated items
items.task: Calculate the impact of current year operations on an S corporation's accumulated adjustments account.
items.stem: Highland Bakery, Inc. is an S corporation with AAA of $30,000 and accumulated earnings and profits of $40,000 from earlier C corporation years. It made one $50,000 distribution to Tess Wu, its only shareholder, whose stock basis is $100,000. How much is a taxable dividend?

why.A: Treats the whole distribution as return of basis. With accumulated earnings and profits, amounts beyond AAA are dividends.
why.B: The first $30,000 comes from AAA and reduces basis. The next $20,000 comes from accumulated earnings and profits and is a dividend.
why.C: Treats all accumulated earnings and profits as distributed; only the $20,000 that exceeds AAA is drawn.
why.D: Treats the entire distribution as a dividend and ignores AAA.

items.rule_line: With accumulated E&P, S distributions come first from AAA, then from E&P as dividends.

items.topic: S corporations — determination of ordinary business income (loss) and separately stated items
items.task: Calculate the impact of current year operations on an S corporation's accumulated adjustments account.
items.stem: Which item does not adjust an S corporation's accumulated adjustments account?
options: Ordinary business income
Separately stated capital gains
Tax-exempt interest income
Nondeductible expenses that are not capital

why.A: Ordinary business income increases AAA, so it does adjust the account.
why.B: Separately stated capital gains increase AAA, so they do adjust the account.
why.C: Tax-exempt income and related expenses are tracked in the other adjustments account, not AAA.
why.D: Nondeductible expenses decrease AAA, so they do adjust the account.

items.rule_line: Tax-exempt income adjusts the other adjustments account, not AAA.

items.topic: S corporations — determination of ordinary business income (loss) and separately stated items
items.task: Calculate the impact of current year operations on an S corporation's accumulated adjustments account.
items.stem: In determining whether a distribution during 2026 comes from AAA, how is the balance at year-end treated?
options: It is computed without regard to a net negative adjustment for the year, so current-year losses do not reduce it
It is reduced by all current-year losses and expenses before any distribution is tested against it
It is computed with regard to the distributions only, ignoring all income items for the year
It is set at $0 whenever the corporation has accumulated earnings and profits from C years

why.A: Under the special rule, AAA for distributions is determined without regard to a net negative adjustment (losses and expenses exceeding income).
why.B: That would count the net negative adjustment; the special rule ignores it.
why.C: Income items increase AAA before distributions are tested.
why.D: AAA is measured regardless of accumulated earnings and profits.

items.rule_line: AAA for distributions is computed without regard to the year's net negative adjustment, so current losses do not reduce it.

items.topic: S corporations — determination of ordinary business income (loss) and separately stated items
items.task: Calculate the impact of current year operations on an S corporation's accumulated adjustments account.
items.stem: Draft Schedule M-2 for Bluff Point, Inc., an S corporation, is shown. The corporation had no other items. Which correction is needed?
options: Remove the $10,000 capital gain from AAA; ending AAA is $112,000
Do not reduce AAA for the $3,000 of nondeductible expenses; ending AAA is $125,000
Do not reduce AAA for distributions; ending AAA is $172,000
Remove the $5,000 of tax-exempt interest from AAA; ending AAA is $117,000

why.A: Separately stated capital gains do increase AAA, so the draft is right on that item.
why.B: Nondeductible expenses reduce AAA, so the draft is right on that item.
why.C: Distributions reduce AAA, so the draft is right on that item.
why.D: Tax-exempt income does not adjust AAA. Correct ending AAA is $40,000 + $120,000 + $10,000 - $3,000 - $50,000 = $117,000.

steps: Draft overstated by the 5,000 tax-exempt interest
items.rule_line: Tax-exempt income does not adjust AAA, though ordinary income, gains, nondeductibles and distributions do.

items.topic: S corporations — determination of ordinary business income (loss) and separately stated items
items.task: Calculate the impact of current year operations on an S corporation's accumulated adjustments account.
items.stem: Pine Terrace, Inc., an S corporation with no accumulated earnings and profits, distributed $45,000 in cash to Uma Ruiz, its only shareholder, whose stock basis was $30,000. The corporation's AAA before the distribution was $60,000. What gain does Uma recognize?

why.A: Treats the entire distribution as tax-free because AAA is large enough; the shareholder's basis is still the limit.
why.B: With no accumulated earnings and profits, distributions are tax-free to the extent of stock basis, then gain. The gain is $45,000 - $30,000 = $15,000 of capital gain; AAA does not override the basis limit.
why.C: Uses the basis as the gain; basis is what is tax-free.
why.D: Treats the whole distribution as gain, ignoring the $30,000 basis.

steps: Tax-free to the extent of basis 30,000
items.rule_line: Without E&P, S distributions are tax-free up to stock basis and gain above it, regardless of AAA.

items.topic: S corporations — determination of ordinary business income (loss) and separately stated items
items.task: Calculate the impact of current year operations on an S corporation's accumulated adjustments account.
items.stem: Two S corporations each have AAA of $60,000 and each distribute $80,000 in cash in 2026 to a sole shareholder whose stock basis is $200,000. Ash Grove, Inc. has accumulated earnings and profits of $25,000 from prior C corporation years. Birch Grove, Inc. has none. Which statement compares the shareholders' results correctly?
options: Both shareholders have a $20,000 dividend
Ash Grove's shareholder has a $25,000 dividend
Ash Grove's shareholder has a $20,000 dividend; Birch Grove's shareholder has no taxable amount
Neither shareholder has a taxable amount, because basis exceeds the distribution

why.A: Birch Grove has no earnings and profits, so nothing is a dividend.
why.B: Only the $20,000 that exceeds AAA is drawn from earnings and profits.
why.C: For Ash Grove, $60,000 comes from AAA and $20,000 from accumulated earnings and profits (a dividend). For Birch Grove, the entire $80,000 reduces basis.
why.D: In a corporation with earnings and profits, the amount beyond AAA is a dividend regardless of basis.

steps: Ash Grove: AAA 60,000 tax-free; E&P 20,000 dividend
Birch Grove: 80,000 reduces basis; no dividend
items.rule_line: Beyond AAA, an S corporation with accumulated E&P pays dividends from E&P; without E&P the excess reduces basis.

items.topic: S corporations — determination of ordinary business income (loss) and separately stated items
items.task: Calculate the impact of current year operations on an S corporation's accumulated adjustments account.
items.stem: Cross Timber, Inc., an S corporation, has accumulated earnings and profits and wants its distributions to be treated as coming first from accumulated earnings and profits, before AAA. What must it do?
options: Make an election with the consent of all affected shareholders
Nothing; the ordering is at the corporation's discretion each year
Obtain consent from holders of more than half of the shares
Convert to a C corporation, since S corporations cannot make this election

why.A: A corporation may elect, with the consent of all affected shareholders, to distribute accumulated earnings and profits first.
why.B: The default order is AAA first, and a change requires an election.
why.C: All affected shareholders must consent, not just a majority.
why.D: S corporations may make the election while remaining S corporations.

items.rule_line: An S corporation may elect to distribute accumulated E&P first with consent of all affected shareholders.

items.topic: S corporations — basis of shareholder's interest
items.task: Calculate a shareholder's stock basis in an S corporation resulting from business operations, cash contributions and cash distributions.
items.stem: Nadia Osei bought her S corporation stock for $50,000 at the start of 2026. For 2026 her share of the corporation's items was ordinary income of $30,000, a long-term capital gain of $6,000, tax-exempt interest of $4,000 and nondeductible expenses of $2,000. She received cash distributions of $20,000. What is her stock basis at year-end?

why.A: Leaves out the $4,000 of tax-exempt interest, which increases stock basis.
why.B: Basis increases for income items (ordinary, capital gain and tax-exempt) and decreases for distributions and nondeductible expenses: $68,000.
why.C: Does not reduce basis for the $2,000 of nondeductible expenses.
why.D: Does not reduce basis for the $20,000 of cash distributions.

items.rule_line: S stock basis increases for income including tax-exempt income and decreases for distributions and nondeductible expenses.

items.topic: S corporations — basis of shareholder's interest
items.task: Calculate a shareholder's stock basis in an S corporation resulting from business operations, cash contributions and cash distributions.
items.stem: Leon Baptiste owns 40% of an S corporation. His stock basis is $25,000 at the start of 2026 and he has no loans to the corporation. His share of the 2026 ordinary business loss is $40,000, and the corporation had no other items. What loss may Leon deduct in 2026, ignoring at-risk and passive activity rules?

why.A: Disallows the entire loss; a loss is allowed up to basis.
why.B: Uses the amount of the suspended loss instead of the amount allowed.
why.C: A shareholder's deductible loss cannot exceed his stock and debt basis. With $25,000 of basis, $25,000 is deductible and $15,000 is suspended.
why.D: Deducts the full loss, ignoring the basis limit.

items.rule_line: An S shareholder's deductible loss is limited to stock plus debt basis, with the excess suspended.

items.topic: S corporations — basis of shareholder's interest
items.task: Calculate changes in a shareholder's debt basis in an S corporation resulting from current year repayment of debt.
items.stem: Priya Nair owns 50% of an S corporation. Her stock basis is $20,000 and she has lent the corporation $30,000 directly (debt basis $30,000). Her share of the 2026 ordinary loss is $45,000. What is her debt basis after the loss is deducted?

why.A: Assumes the entire $45,000 loss reduces debt basis. Stock basis absorbs the first $20,000.
why.B: The loss first reduces stock basis to $0 ($20,000), and the remaining $25,000 reduces debt basis to $5,000.
why.C: This is the $25,000 of loss charged to debt basis, not the debt basis that remains.
why.D: Leaves debt basis unchanged; the loss exceeds stock basis, so debt basis is reduced.

steps: Loss 45,000 - stock basis 20,000 = 25,000 charged to debt basis
items.rule_line: S losses reduce stock basis first, then debt basis for the excess.

items.topic: S corporations — basis of shareholder's interest
items.task: Calculate changes in a shareholder's debt basis in an S corporation resulting from current year repayment of debt.
items.stem: Ivan Petrov made a $50,000 direct loan to his S corporation. Prior losses reduced his basis in the note to $30,000. In 2026 the corporation repaid $25,000 of the note (evidenced by a written note). What gain does Ivan recognize?

why.A: Treats the repayment as a tax-free return of capital; repayment of a note whose basis was reduced produces gain.
why.B: Subtracts the repayment from the remaining basis, which measures leftover basis rather than gain.
why.C: The repayment is 50% of the note. The basis in the repaid portion is 50% x $30,000 = $15,000, so the gain is $25,000 - $15,000 = $10,000.
why.D: Recognizes the whole repayment as gain, ignoring the basis in the repaid part.

items.rule_line: Repayment of a note whose basis was reduced produces gain in proportion to the repaid share of the note.

items.topic: S corporations — basis of shareholder's interest
items.task: Calculate changes in a shareholder's debt basis in an S corporation resulting from current year repayment of debt.
items.stem: Mona Reyes has a note from her S corporation with an original basis of $40,000, which prior losses reduced to $10,000. In 2026 her share of the corporation's net income is $50,000. Ignoring distributions, how much of the $50,000 increases her stock basis?

why.A: Assumes the income only restores debt basis.
why.B: Net income first restores debt basis to its original $40,000 (a $30,000 restoration). Only the remaining $20,000 increases stock basis.
why.C: This is the amount that restores debt basis, not the amount that increases stock basis.
why.D: Applies all the income to stock basis; debt basis must be restored first.

items.rule_line: Net S income first restores debt basis to its original amount before increasing stock basis.

items.stem: Which item decreases a shareholder's basis in S corporation stock?
options: The shareholder's share of tax-exempt interest
The shareholder's share of a separately stated capital gain
A cash contribution the shareholder makes to the corporation
The shareholder's share of nondeductible expenses, such as fines

why.A: Tax-exempt income increases stock basis.
why.B: Separately stated income items increase stock basis.
why.C: Capital contributions increase stock basis.
why.D: Nondeductible expenses that are not capital reduce stock basis.

items.rule_line: Nondeductible expenses reduce S stock basis, while tax-exempt income, capital gains and contributions increase it.

items.topic: S corporations — basis of shareholder's interest
items.task: Calculate a shareholder's stock basis in an S corporation resulting from business operations, cash contributions and cash distributions.
items.stem: Sam Ortega owns 50% of an S corporation for the entire year. In 2026 the corporation donated land (adjusted basis $20,000, fair market value $60,000) to a qualified charity. By how much does the donation reduce Sam's stock basis?

why.A: Assumes no reduction because the property was donated instead of paid in cash.
why.B: Basis reduces by the shareholder's pro rata share of the property's adjusted basis: 50% x $20,000 = $10,000.
why.C: Uses the whole adjusted basis; Sam is responsible only for his 50% share.
why.D: Uses his share of fair market value, which is what passes through for the charitable deduction, not the basis reduction.

items.rule_line: A property charitable donation by an S corporation reduces shareholder basis by the shareholder's share of the property's adjusted basis.

items.topic: S corporations — basis of shareholder's interest
items.task: Calculate changes in a shareholder's debt basis in an S corporation resulting from current year repayment of debt.
items.stem: Two unrelated 50% shareholders of an S corporation each have stock basis of $10,000. Xavier lent the corporation $40,000 directly. Yara guaranteed a $40,000 bank loan to the corporation but paid nothing on it. Each shareholder's share of the 2026 loss is $60,000. How much more loss may Xavier deduct than Yara?

why.A: Assumes a guarantee gives the same basis as a direct loan.
why.B: Compares Yara's disallowed loss with the debt basis; it does not give the difference in deductions.
why.C: Xavier's basis is $10,000 stock plus $40,000 debt = $50,000, so he deducts $50,000. Yara's guarantee creates no basis, so she deducts only $10,000. The difference is $40,000.
why.D: Adds the stock basis to the difference; the difference in deductible loss is only the extra debt basis.

items.rule_line: A shareholder loan to the corporation creates debt basis, but a mere guarantee does not.

items.task: Calculate a shareholder's stock basis in an S corporation resulting from business operations, cash contributions and cash distributions.
items.stem: Draft basis worksheet for Petra Lund's S corporation stock for 2026 is shown. Petra's share of tax-exempt interest was $4,000 and it was omitted; all other items are correct. Which correction is needed?
options: Remove the $6,000 capital gain, since separately stated gains do not increase basis; ending basis is $58,000
Do not reduce basis for the $2,000 of nondeductible expenses; ending basis is $66,000
Add the $4,000 of tax-exempt interest; ending basis is $68,000
Do not reduce basis for distributions, because AAA covers them; ending basis is $84,000

why.B: Nondeductible expenses reduce stock basis, so the draft is right on this item.

why.D: Distributions reduce stock basis even when AAA covers them, so the draft is right on this item.

items.rule_line: Tax-exempt interest increases S stock basis, so it must be added; the other worksheet items are correct.

items.stem: An S corporation shareholder has a $60,000 loss allocated to her. In which order are the limitations applied in determining how much loss she may deduct?

At-risk first, then basis, then the passive activity limits
Passive activity first, then at-risk, then basis
Basis and passive activity together, and at-risk not at all

why.A: The loss must first be within stock and debt basis, then at-risk, then passive loss limitations.
why.B: Basis is the first limitation.
why.C: The passive rules are applied last, not first.
why.D: The at-risk limits apply to S corporation shareholders too.

items.stem: Wanda Kroll contributed equipment with an adjusted basis of $12,000 and a fair market value of $30,000 to her S corporation as a capital contribution without receiving additional stock. By how much does the contribution increase her stock basis?

why.D: Uses fair market value; the shareholder adds her adjusted basis.

items.rule_line: A capital contribution of property increases stock basis by the shareholder's adjusted basis in the property.

items.stem: Willow Springs, Inc. converted from a C corporation to an S corporation effective January 1, 2020. In 2026 it sold an asset that was appreciated when it converted. Which statement is correct?

items.stem: Pete Lindgren liquidated his entire partnership interest, in which his basis was $60,000, and received only $45,000 in cash. The partnership has no unrealized receivables or inventory. What loss does Pete recognize?

why.A: Assumes losses are never recognized on a distribution; in a liquidation for money only, the loss is recognized.
why.B: In a liquidation, a loss is recognized only if the partner receives just money, unrealized receivables and inventory. Here he receives only cash, so the loss is $60,000 - $45,000 = $15,000.
why.C: Uses the cash received as the loss.
why.D: Uses the whole basis as the loss without offsetting the cash received.

items.rule_line: In a liquidation receiving only money, unrealized receivables and inventory, the partner recognizes a loss for basis minus cash.

items.stem: Quinn Alder sold her entire partnership interest for $80,000 in cash. Her basis in the interest, including her $20,000 share of partnership liabilities, was $50,000, and the buyer assumed her $20,000 share of liabilities. Of her gain, $15,000 is attributable to unrealized receivables. How much capital gain does Quinn recognize?

why.A: Uses only the ordinary income portion.
why.B: Amount realized is $80,000 + $20,000 = $100,000, and the total gain is $50,000. Subtract the $15,000 ordinary income from unrealized receivables: $35,000 is capital gain.
why.C: Treats the whole $50,000 as capital gain, ignoring the ordinary income on unrealized receivables.
why.D: Adds the ordinary income to the gain instead of subtracting it.

items.rule_line: On sale of a partnership interest, gain from unrealized receivables is ordinary, and amount realized includes liability relief.

options: The part attributable to the partnership's goodwill
The part attributable to the partner's share of liabilities
No part of the gain, since the sale of an interest is capital gain in full
The part attributable to the partnership's unrealized receivables

why.A: Goodwill generally produces capital gain when a partnership interest is sold.
why.B: The share of liabilities affects amount realized and basis, not character.
why.C: Amounts attributable to unrealized receivables and inventory are ordinary.
why.D: Amounts attributable to unrealized receivables and inventory items are taxed as ordinary income on a sale of an interest.

items.rule_line: On sale of a partnership interest, amounts from unrealized receivables and inventory are ordinary; goodwill gain is capital.

items.stem: Bea Norwood bought Cal's partnership interest for $150,000. Her share of the partnership's basis in its assets (inside basis) is $100,000. The partnership has a basis adjustment election in effect. What is the basis adjustment to the partnership's assets with respect to Bea?

why.A: Assumes no adjustment, which is the result without the election.
why.B: With the election, Bea's share of asset basis is increased by the difference between her outside basis (cost) and her share of inside basis: $50,000.
why.C: Uses her share of inside basis as the adjustment.
why.D: Uses her cost as the adjustment.

steps: Cost 150,000 - share of inside basis 100,000 = 50,000 increase
items.rule_line: With a section 754 election, the transferee's basis adjustment is her outside basis minus her share of inside basis.

options: A partner buys an interest when the partnership's adjusted basis exceeds asset value by $200,000
A partner gives his interest to a child as a gift when the assets are worth much more than basis
A partner buys an interest when the partnership's adjusted basis in its assets exceeds their fair market value by $300,000
A new partner contributes cash to the partnership for a new interest

why.A: The loss is below the $250,000 threshold, so no mandatory adjustment applies.
why.B: A gift is not a sale, exchange or death transfer, so the adjustment rules do not apply.
why.C: A mandatory adjustment applies on a transfer if the partnership has a substantial built-in loss (more than $250,000).
why.D: A contribution to the partnership is not a transfer of an existing interest.

items.rule_line: A mandatory basis adjustment applies on a transfer if the partnership has a substantial built-in loss over $250,000.

options: Include the $20,000 of liabilities assumed in the amount realized; total gain is $50,000
Add another $20,000 to basis for the liabilities; total gain is $10,000
Leave the gain at $30,000, because liabilities do not affect a sale of an interest
Increase the gain to $70,000, by adding the $20,000 of liabilities to both sides

why.A: Relief from partnership liabilities is part of the amount realized, so the amount realized is $100,000 and the gain is $50,000.
why.B: Her basis already includes the $20,000 share of liabilities, so adding it again double counts and understates the gain.
why.C: Liability relief increases amount realized on the sale of a partnership interest.
why.D: Adding it to both sides cancels out; only the amount realized changes.

items.rule_line: Liability relief is part of the amount realized on the sale of a partnership interest, and basis already includes the liability share.

items.stem: Two entities each own land with an adjusted basis of $30,000 and a fair market value of $100,000, and each distributes the land to a 50% owner as a current distribution. One entity is an S corporation and the other a partnership. Which statement compares the entity-level results correctly?
options: Both entities recognize a $70,000 gain on distributing the land to a 50% owner
Neither entity recognizes gain, because both are pass-through entities that are not themselves taxed
The partnership recognizes a $70,000 gain and the S corporation recognizes no gain on the distribution
The S corporation recognizes a $70,000 gain that passes through to shareholders; the partnership generally recognizes none

why.A: The partnership does not recognize gain on a current distribution of property.
why.B: An S corporation is taxed like a corporation on the distribution of appreciated property.
why.C: The results are reversed.
why.D: A corporation, including an S corporation, recognizes gain on distributing appreciated property. A partnership generally recognizes no gain on a current distribution.

items.rule_line: An S corporation recognizes gain on distributing appreciated property, while a partnership generally recognizes none on a current distribution.

why.A: Carries over the partnership's basis, which applies to current distributions but not to a liquidation.
why.B: In a liquidation the partner's basis in distributed property (other than money) is his remaining outside basis after the cash: $80,000 - $20,000 = $60,000.
why.C: Uses the whole outside basis without reducing it by the cash.
why.D: Uses fair market value, which does not determine a partner's basis in distributed property.

steps: Outside basis 80,000 - cash 20,000 = 60,000 allocated to the land
items.rule_line: In a liquidation the partner's basis in distributed property is remaining outside basis after cash.

items.stem: Tara Wolfe liquidated her partnership interest, in which her basis was $25,000. She received $20,000 in cash and land with a partnership adjusted basis of $30,000 and a fair market value of $90,000. Which statement is correct?
options: She recognizes no gain, and her basis in the land is $30,000
She recognizes a $25,000 gain because the cash and land basis exceed her basis
She recognizes no gain, and her basis in the land is $5,000
She recognizes a $65,000 gain, and her basis in the land is $90,000

why.A: The land's basis is limited to her remaining outside basis after the cash.
why.B: Gain arises only if the cash exceeds her outside basis.
why.C: Cash of $20,000 does not exceed her $25,000 basis, so no gain. The land takes her remaining basis of $5,000.
why.D: Fair market value is not used, and no gain arises here.

items.rule_line: In a liquidation with cash below basis, no gain arises and the property takes the remaining outside basis.

Three years later the partnership sold the land for $130,000. Using the traditional method, how much of the gain is allocated to Ben?

why.A: Allocates all gain to Ann.
why.B: The $60,000 built-in gain is allocated to Ann first. The remaining $30,000 of gain ($130,000 - $100,000) is shared 50/50, so Ben gets $15,000.
why.C: Splits the total $90,000 gain equally, ignoring the built-in gain that belongs to the contributor.
why.D: This is Ann's total gain, not Ben's.

items.rule_line: Under the traditional method, built-in gain on contributed property is allocated to the contributor before remaining gain is shared.

items.stem: Which special allocation of partnership items among partners is most likely to be respected for federal tax purposes?
options: An allocation of 90% of depreciation to one partner, with capital accounts maintained, liquidation by capital accounts and deficit restoration
An allocation of tax-exempt income to the partner in the lowest bracket that does not change any partner's capital account or distributions at all
An allocation of income to one partner in one year and offsetting loss in the next, made only to change the partners' tax brackets
An allocation of gain that follows equal shares while the partners' capital accounts and distributions follow a 70/30 split of profits

why.A: An allocation has substantial economic effect when it follows the partners' economic arrangement, including capital accounts, liquidation by capital accounts and deficit restoration.
why.B: An allocation with no effect on the economic deal does not have economic effect.
why.C: An allocation that merely shifts tax consequences without changing amounts the partners receive is not substantial.
why.D: The allocation disagrees with the partners' economic arrangement, so it would not be respected.

items.rule_line: A special allocation is respected only with substantial economic effect, following capital accounts and the partners' economic deal.

December 31, because Moe has the calendar year and partnerships must use the year of the smallest partner
Either year, at the partners' choice on Form 1065
June 30, the tax year of the partners owning a majority interest in profits and capital

why.A: There is no default of December 31 when a majority-interest year exists.
why.B: There is no rule favoring the smaller partner.
why.C: The majority interest rule controls unless another permitted year is elected.
why.D: A partnership generally adopts the tax year of partners who own more than 50% of profits and capital.

options: Both have $30,000 of ordinary income, because any interest received for services is compensation
Neither has income, because interests received in partnerships are not taxed on receipt
Rex has $30,000 of ordinary income, while Ola generally has no income if the profits interest conditions are met
Ola has ordinary income, and Rex has none because a capital interest is not compensation

why.B: A capital interest received for services is taxed at its value.
why.C: A capital interest received for services is compensation at its value. A profits interest generally is not taxed on receipt under the IRS safe harbor.

items.stem: Sol Fernandez is the only member of Fernandez Landscaping, LLC, a domestic limited liability company. It has made no entity classification election. How is the LLC classified for federal income tax purposes, and how does Sol report its income?
options: It is disregarded, and Sol reports the income and expenses on his own return, such as Schedule C
It is a partnership, and Sol reports his share on a Schedule K-1 from Form 1065
It is a C corporation, and Sol reports only the dividends he receives from it
It is an S corporation, and Sol reports his share on a Schedule K-1 from Form 1120-S

why.A: A domestic single-member LLC with no election is a disregarded entity, so its owner reports the activity directly.
why.B: A partnership requires at least two members.
why.C: A corporation classification requires an election or an incorporated entity.
why.D: An S corporation requires a valid S election, which the LLC has not made.

items.rule_line: A domestic single-member LLC with no election is disregarded, and its owner reports income on his own return.

options: January 1, 2026, the start of the tax year
May 20, 2026, the filing date only
March 20, 2026, which is 61 days before the filing date
March 6, 2026, which is 75 days before the filing date

why.A: Retroactivity is limited to 75 days, not to the beginning of the year.
why.B: The effective date may be earlier, up to 75 days before the filing date.
why.C: The rule allows 75 days, not 61 days.
why.D: An election may be effective up to 75 days before it is filed, and up to 12 months after.

items.rule_line: A Form 8832 entity classification election may be effective up to 75 days before the filing date.

items.stem: Harbor View Partners, LLC has three members and is taxed as a partnership. It wants to be taxed as an S corporation beginning in 2027. Which statement is correct?
options: It must first dissolve the LLC and organize a new corporation under state law
It can file Form 2553, and the filing is treated as an election to be classified as an association as well
It cannot make an S election, because LLCs are not eligible for S status
It must file Form 8832 and Form 2553 together, and S status is effective only after two years

why.A: No state law conversion is required.
why.B: A timely S election by an eligible entity is also treated as a deemed election to be taxed as a corporation.
why.C: An eligible LLC may elect S status if it meets the requirements.
why.D: Form 2553 alone is enough, and there is no two-year delay.

items.rule_line: A timely Form 2553 by an eligible LLC is also treated as an election to be taxed as a corporation.

The change is not permitted after a corporation election
The change is generally not permitted before 60 months after the election's effective date
The change is permitted after 12 months by filing Form 8832

why.B: A new election is allowed after the 60-month period.

why.D: The waiting period is 60 months, not 12.

For all federal taxes the LLC is disregarded, so Tess reports the employees' payroll taxes on her own return as an individual
The LLC is treated as a partnership for income tax and as a corporation for employment tax
The LLC is treated as a corporation for income tax and disregarded for employment tax

why.B: Employment taxes for wages paid to employees are the entity's responsibility.
why.C: A single-member LLC cannot be a partnership.

items.rule_line: A single-member LLC is disregarded for income tax but treated as a corporation for employment taxes on its employees.

options: It spends a small portion of its budget on lobbying that is not substantial
It charges reasonable fees for the educational programs it offers
It pays reasonable salaries to its employees for their services
A portion of its net earnings benefits its founder, who is a private individual

why.A: Insubstantial lobbying does not disqualify a charitable organization.
why.B: Reasonable fees for exempt activities are permitted.
why.C: Reasonable compensation is not private inurement.
why.D: Exemption requires that no part of net earnings inure to the benefit of a private shareholder or individual.

items.rule_line: Exemption is lost if any net earnings inure to a private individual; insubstantial lobbying, reasonable fees and reasonable salaries are permitted.

why.C: A charity serves a broad public purpose, not the common business interests of members.
why.D: A social club is organized for pleasure and recreation of its members.

items.rule_line: Chambers of commerce and similar groups promoting common business interests qualify as business leagues.

why.B: A union is not organized for charitable purposes.
why.C: Labor unions are described in the category for labor, agricultural and horticultural organizations.
why.D: A union's exemption is under its own labor category.

items.rule_line: Labor unions qualify as labor, agricultural or horticultural organizations.

Exclude the dividends but no specific deduction is allowed, making UBTI $25,000

Add the $10,000 of dividends to directly connected expenses, making UBTI $25,000

why.A: Dividends are excluded passive income, so they should come out.

why.D: Dividends are not expenses; they are excluded from income.

items.rule_line: Dividends are excluded from UBTI, and the $1,000 specific deduction applies.

For 2026 its fiduciary accounting income was $40,000, and trustee fees of $3,000 are charged against that income. It also had a $10,000 capital gain that is allocated to principal. What amount does the sole income beneficiary include in income from the trust?

why.A: Distributable net income is $37,000 (income less fees; the gain allocated to principal is excluded). A simple trust's beneficiary reports the income required to be distributed, limited to DNI.
why.B: Ignores the $3,000 of trustee fees charged against income.
why.C: Adds the capital gain that is allocated to principal and is not distributed.
why.D: Adds the capital gain and ignores the fees.

steps: The $10,000 gain stays in the trust (taxed to the trust)
items.rule_line: A simple trust's beneficiary reports income required to be distributed, limited to DNI, after fees and excluding principal gains.

items.stem: Mesa Ridge Corp. began 2026 with an accumulated earnings and profits deficit of $100,000 and had current earnings and profits of $30,000 for 2026, earned evenly. It distributed $20,000 on July 1 to one shareholder and $20,000 on December 1 to another. How much of the December 1 distribution is a dividend?

why.A: Nets the current earnings against the accumulated deficit.
why.B: Current earnings and profits are allocated pro rata among the year's distributions: $30,000 x $20,000 / $40,000 = $15,000 per distribution. The accumulated deficit does not reduce current earnings and profits.
why.C: Treats the whole distribution as a dividend.
why.D: Assigns all current earnings and profits to the December distribution.

steps: Current E&P allocated 30,000 x (20,000 / 40,000) = 15,000 to each distribution
items.rule_line: Current E&P is allocated pro rata among distributions during the year and is not reduced by an accumulated deficit.

For 2026 his share of the S corporation's ordinary income is $30,000, and he receives a $10,000 distribution. He has no debt basis. What is his stock basis at year-end after the suspended loss is deducted?

why.A: Basis is increased by income ($35,000), then reduced by the distribution ($25,000), then by the previously suspended loss, which is now allowed: $13,000.
why.B: Does not reduce basis for the distribution.
why.C: Does not reduce basis for the previously suspended loss that is now deductible.
why.D: Ignores both the distribution and the suspended loss.

items.rule_line: S basis increases by income, decreases by distributions, then by previously suspended losses now allowed.

why.B: Each partner's share is $40,000, limited to basis. Abe deducts $10,000 and Bea deducts $40,000, a total of $50,000.
why.C: Uses Bea's whole basis rather than her $40,000 share of the loss.
why.D: Allows the entire loss, ignoring basis limits.

items.rule_line: Each partner's loss is limited to his own basis, so the total deductible is the sum of each partner's allowed amount.

items.topic: C corporations — computation of taxable income, tax liability and allowable credits

items.stem: Two corporations each receive $200,000 of dividends from a 10%-owned domestic corporation and qualify for the 50% dividends-received deduction. Lark Co. has taxable income of $150,000 before the deduction. Moss Co. has taxable income of $60,000 before the deduction. Which statement is correct?
options: Both deduct $100,000, because the taxable-income limit does not apply to dividends of 10%-owned corporations
Lark deducts $100,000 and Moss deducts $30,000
Lark's deduction is limited to $75,000, and Moss deducts the full $100,000, which creates a net operating loss
Both are limited to 50% of taxable income, so Lark deducts $75,000 and Moss deducts $30,000

why.A: The limit applies unless the full deduction would create a loss.
why.B: Lark is limited to 50% of taxable income, and Moss is not limited because the full deduction creates a loss.
why.C: The taxable-income limit does not apply if the full deduction would create or increase a net operating loss. It does not for Lark but does for Moss.
why.D: The loss exception allows Moss the full deduction.

steps: Lark: 50% x 150,000 = 75,000; full 100,000 would leave 50,000 of income, so no loss and the limit applies
Moss: 50% x 200,000 = 100,000 exceeds taxable income 60,000, so it creates a loss and the limit does not apply
items.rule_line: The DRD taxable-income limit does not apply if the full deduction would create or increase an NOL.

items.stem: Orchard Bay Supply, Inc. was formed and began business on January 1, 2026, and intended to be an S corporation from that date. Its shareholders signed Form 2553, but it was not filed until July 10, 2026. The corporation otherwise met every S requirement. Which statement is correct?
options: The election is effective January 1, 2026, because Form 2553 may be filed at any time during the tax year and is still timely
The election is permanently invalid, because a late Form 2553 cannot be corrected by the IRS under any procedure
The election is effective for 2026 but only for the portion of the year after the July 10 filing date
The election is not effective for 2026 unless the IRS grants late-election relief, which requires reasonable cause and a timely request

why.A: The election must be filed by the 15th day of the third month to be effective for that year.
why.B: Relief provisions allow a late election to be treated as timely.
why.C: An election is effective for the whole year or not at all for that year, not from the filing date.
why.D: An election filed after the 15th day of the third month is late. Rev. Proc. 2013-30 offers relief within 3 years and 75 days of the intended effective date when reasonable cause exists.

items.rule_line: A Form 2553 filed after the 15th day of the third month is late and needs IRS late-election relief for that year.

items.stem: Wells Corridor Corp. completely liquidated in 2026, and Jon Ames, its only shareholder, received $250,000 in cash. Jon's stock basis is $80,000 and he has held the stock for five years. His draft return reports the $170,000 as an ordinary dividend. Which correction is needed?
options: Report a $250,000 long-term capital gain, with no basis offset
Report a $170,000 long-term capital gain, because a complete liquidation is treated as a sale of the stock
Report a $170,000 dividend, because liquidating distributions are dividends to the extent of value over basis
Report no gain, because liquidating distributions are a tax-free return of basis until basis is recovered, and the excess is deferred

why.A: Gain is measured after subtracting the $80,000 basis.
why.B: In a complete liquidation the shareholder computes gain or loss on the exchange of stock, which here is long-term capital gain.
why.C: Liquidating distributions are exchanges, not dividends.
why.D: The full gain is recognized in the liquidation year.

steps: Amount received 250,000 - basis 80,000 = 170,000 long-term capital gain
items.rule_line: A complete liquidation is treated as a sale of stock, so the shareholder reports capital gain after subtracting basis.

Report no gain, and carry the $15,000 excess forward to increase basis next year
Report a $15,000 capital gain, because cash in excess of basis is gain from the sale of the partnership interest
Report a $45,000 capital gain, because the entire distribution is gain

steps: Character: capital gain, absent unrealized receivables or inventory
items.rule_line: Money distributed in excess of partnership basis is gain from the sale of the interest, taxed as capital gain.
